articles.content:
With his unguarded lyricism and earnest delivery, the late singer-songwriter is having a moment among a generation that fetishizes unrequited desire

S ydney Tripoli has collected Jeff Buckley memorabilia since 2019. She keeps her collection of T-shirts, posters, vinyl and other merch celebrating the late singer-songwriter in what she affectionately calls her “Buckley box”. The 27-year-old scours eBay and resale sites for these pieces; lately she’s noticed the prices “skyrocket”.

“During the pandemic, it was impossible to find Jeff Buckley shirts. Now they’re everywhere on Depop,” said Tripoli, who works as an actor in Los Angeles. “Now [my collection] is worth thousands of dollars.”

Tripoli was born in 1999, two years after Buckley’s death at age 30 from an accidental drowning in the Mississippi River. She first heard his moody, blues-tinged music as a child. In college she wrote a paper on 1994’s Grace, the only album released during the artist’s lifetime. She felt it was the perfect soundtrack for that time in her life: equal parts horny and romantic, ecstatic one moment and hopeless the next.

Though Buckley was solidly a product of generation X, with slacker posturing and a distaste for the music industry’s corporate trappings, his songs seem to speak to members of gen Z like Tripoli.

Buckley’s impassioned, unguarded lyrics made him an instant critical darling, but initial sales of Grace were slow, perhaps because such earnestness seemed out of step with the era’s more grungier tendencies. But a spate of posthumous releases helped find him new fans. In 2004, the teen drama The OC used his cover of Leonard Cohen’s Hallelujah as an emotional needledrop at the end of its first season. The same song hit the top of the iTunes charts in 2008 after American Idol judges Simon Cowell and Randy Jackson called it their favorite version.

David Bowie once called Grace his “desert island” album; Bob Dylan said Buckley was the greatest songwriter of the 90s. Brad Pitt tried and failed to materialize a Buckley biopic he wanted to star in, going so far as to invite the musician’s mother to his wedding with Jennifer Aniston.

Now Buckley is once again finding new fans. Streams of his songs have steadily ticked upwards since 2022, just as the oldest of gen Z reached their mid-20s. It’s a fitting renaissance for a nostalgia-soaked generation who have also propelled romance novels to the top of bestseller lists. It’s a group that came of age during Covid lockdowns, that is less likely to date or enter relationships. They fetishize the act of wanting and unrequited desire.

Chuchu Zulu, a 19-year-old political science student in Orlando, attributes this popularity to “the yearning Jeff Buckley craze”. Yearning is a slow burn, an antidote to on-demand culture. Buckley’s ornate, louche music is fundamentally anti-algorithm. “We don’t really have a Jeff Buckley for our time,” Zulu added.

Data from the music analytics company found that Buckley’s belting breakup anthem Lover, You Should Have Come Over has been used in more than 500,000 TikToks this year. It has been streamed more than 25m times in the past month. A TikTok representative shared that searches for “Buckley” have increased more than 30% in the last two weeks.

Three of his tracks are on the melancholic – and popular, with more than half a million followers – Spotify playlist “yearner final boss”, alongside adult contemporary staples such as The Goo Goo Dolls’ Iris and Prince’s Purple Rain.

Yaw Appiah, 19, studies journalism at Rutgers University, where he writes music reviews for the school paper and works on its college radio station. He said Buckley epitomizes “the yearning epidemic”. “It’s such a coveted emotion,” he said. “It’s so prevalent all around us that it leads us to gravitate towards pieces of media that feature yearning.”

Renewed interest in Buckley has been buoyed by the documentary It’s Never Over, Jeff Buckley, which premiered at last year’s Sundance film festival and is now on HBO. Experimental musician Rebecca Moore, who dated Buckley and inspired much of Grace, spoke at length for the first time in the film, humanizing her oft-mythologized ex. She described Buckley as an animal lover who would “throw himself over the counter at a bodega to hug a cute cat”, but said that he struggled with mental health issues. In their last phone conversation just days before his death, he told her he might be bipolar.

Erika Freiman, a 22-year-old from Vancouver, works part-time in a record store. She said Grace is a bestseller, particularly among people her age. “It always sells, especially in the fall because it’s super cozy and emotionally vulnerable,” Freiman said. “It’s super romantic, too. I think if someone buys you Grace for your birthday, it says a lot.”

The unbridled candor of Buckley’s lyrics speaks to a generation that’s literate in therapy speak but disillusioned by its platitudes. “A lot of people are yearners, but they’re too scared to show it,” Freiman said. “You can hide behind a screen and comment on TikTok saying, ‘This is so me,’ but people have a hard time doing it in real life. People want that connection, and this generation is just so lacking of it. It doesn’t really happen, so it’s kind of like a fantasy.”

Tripoli, from Los Angeles, added that Buckley’s songs are the antithesis of the misogynistic drivel that comes out of the manosphere, which young women are all too familiar with in 2026. “The concept of a man in his 20s describing a woman with such beauty and respect is so rare,” she said. “Even when it has some of his songs with more sexual undertones, I feel like it’s still so pure and whole.” (Joan Wasser, a musician who performs as Joan As Police Woman, dated Buckley and described him in the documentary as “a really staunch defender of woman”.)

Sammi Katzmann and Jenna Pascale are a cello-saxophone duo based in New York who go by KatzPascale. The pair have covered Buckley’s songs in concert. Both are gen Z, but they think the music resonates with people of all ages.

“I feel that it’s timeless, and it just happens to be having a revival moment right now because it’s so good,” Katzmann said. “I was in Paris the other day, and they were playing Jeff Buckley the entire time, everywhere.”

articles.content:
Rockstar Games’ brilliant 18-rated criminal caper is stuffed with sex, drugs and violence. It is the most explicit game I’ve ever played – and it really is not for kids

I am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “ no way” . Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty.

Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. It is an incredible creative and technical feat, conjuring a realistic-looking and exhaustively detailed virtual Florida filled with every kind of filth and criminality you could imagine. It is brilliant, entertainingly observed and even sometimes unexpectedly touching, largely thanks to a central love story between the player couple , Jason and Lucia. It is lewd, violent and frequently hilarious. It is also absolutely full of stuff that I really would not want my 10 and seven-year-old boys to see or hear. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating.

Everyone knows that Grand Theft Auto is a violent game. It’s about crime and criminals, and VI’s story is about two fugitives in Vice City and the absolute dirtbags they meet along the way. You steal cars, run drugs, shoot cops and rival criminals and hold up gas stations; you kill hundreds of people over the course of the game. There are executions, brutal police raids and depictions of torture. None of that is particularly new, but it’s still pretty hardcore for, say, a nine-year-old. Plenty of millennials played Grand Theft Auto when we were underage, but video games are an awful lot more realistic now than they were 20 years ago; graphic violence on a PlayStation 2 from the 00s looks very different from graphic violence on a PlayStation 5 in 2026.

Let’s leave the violence aside for a minute, though: there is also a lot more explicit sexual content in GTA VI than any previous GTA game, or any other video game period. 2004’s Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas was briefly pulled from sale because it contained a sex minigame that you couldn’t even access without hacking the game’s code. GTA VI, meanwhile, contains a LOT of sex that is in no way hidden, including between the two main characters. On another character’s laptop, there in a browsable in-game version of OnlyFans that pulls exactly no punches. There is full-frontal nudity, male and female. One mission takes place during a porn shoot, several others in strip clubs and bars, one in a hotel where you can burst into the wrong room to find an ongoing orgy or a bunch of people eating sushi off a naked body. I don’t personally fancy explaining any of this to my kids!

Then there’s the drugs. You run drugs, you steal drugs, you sell drugs and you take drugs. Pretty much everyone in Vice City really enjoys their coke; there are copious party scenes where powder is everywhere, and the player characters can partake if you want. Chapter 3 of the game is literally titled “Tits Ass Drug Money”. You might read all of this and think, my teenager has seen worse. That’s perfectly fair – but this is not stuff a 10- or 12-year-old can really contextualise, in my opinion (and the opinion of the ratings boards). If you think your child is too young to watch Breaking Bad, they are definitely too young for Grand Theft Auto VI .

Even the in-game TV and radio is full of vulgar humour. On a phone-in show, I heard a caller and the host vamp extensively about her boyfriend’s penis’s resemblance, in size and smell, to a chicken nugget. A psychic medium considers whether people can still indulge their foot fetishes in the afterlife, in incorporeal form. One of the in-game podcasts stars two female hosts talking in explicit detail about how attracted they are to various famous murderers. Walking past random pedestrians on the street you will frequently hear people talking at length about their dicks and what they have recently done with them. I am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty.

Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. It is an incredible creative and technical feat, conjuring a realistic-looking and exhaustively detailed virtual Florida filled with every kind of filth and criminality you could imagine. It is brilliant, entertainingly observed and even sometimes unexpectedly touching, largely thanks to a central love story between the player couple , Jason and Lucia. It is lewd, violent and frequently hilarious. It is also absolutely full of stuff that I really would not want my 10 and seven-year-old boys to see or hear. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating.

Everyone knows that Grand Theft Auto is a violent game. It’s about crime and criminals, and VI’s story is about two fugitives in Vice City and the absolute dirtbags they meet along the way. articles.content:
The Irish singer-songwriter would have turned 60 in early December. To mark the occasion, we revisit the best of a catalogue that’s far more than a certain Prince cover

This suitably uncompromising opener to the lengthy Faith and Courage offers a collage of radio static, Indian-inspired beats, dub bassline and whispered vocals. More importantly, it’s fantastic: you might call it trip-hop were Sinéad O’Connor’s vocal not so intense as to negate any potential for relaxation on the part of the listener.

From O’Connor’s final album, I’m Not Bossy, I’m the Boss – she abandoned an almost-complete follow-up with producer David Holmes after the death of her son – The Voice of My Doctor is grinding, distorted blues rock. Its lyric, a saga of infidelity delivered with real fury, references Nothing Compares 2 U.

Am I Not Your Girl? now seems wildly ahead of its time; a collection of covers of American Broadway, jazz and film standards (before such things became reliable pop staples), all fabulously orchestrated. Here, the blasting John Barry-style brass presages the 90s easy-listening revival, but the real drama lies in O’Connor’s astonishing vocal.

An explosion of life-affirming joy in a catalogue not much given to that kind of thing, the ramshackle but wildly catchy 4th and Vine is an untrammelled delight. Extra points for the simple-but-great video, featuring a beaming O’Connor and band belting it out in a packed Irish pub.

O’Connor was a friend of Kurt Cobain: after his death, she stripped back Nirvana’s All Apologies to almost nothing beyond an acoustic guitar and a vocal that replaces the original’s pained yowl with a kind of fierce, pure whisper. It is utterly haunting.

As close to a straightforward pop track as O’Connor ever recorded, the lissom funk of I Want Your (Hands on Me) bears the faint influence of Jam and Lewis in its production, and of their former employee Prince in its forthright lyrical approach to seduction. It’s sonically of its time, but a total banger nonetheless.

A stark, potent depiction of institutionalised racism and poverty in Thatcher-era Britain (“not the mythical land of Madame George and roses”) that still hits hard nearly 40 years on. “These are dangerous days – to say what you feel is to dig your own grave,” she notes, two years before her infamous SNL appearance.

The soaring melody and warm arrangement (it was co-produced by Brian Eno) can’t quite mask the sense of unease engendered by the lyrics. A saga of birth, love, hatred and regret, they’re oblique enough to be open to interpretation – is it about mother-daughter relations? – but powerful enough to knock you sideways.

An Irish folk standard with roots in a 17th-century poem, O’Connor’s take on I Am Stretched on Your Grave welds a stark, largely a cappella reading of the song to a baggy-era breakbeat. It’s an improbable idea that somehow succeeds in amping up its stark grief: you couldn’t imagine anyone dancing to it.

An entirely original break-up song, apparently inspired by O’Connor’s relationship with Peter Gabriel, the gently trip-hop influenced Thank You for Hearing Me occupies a complex but believable emotional space. It’s all gratitude and fond recollection until the final verse, when a note of darkness, a faint hint of screw-you, clouds the picture.

O’Connor’s debut single arrived in the autumn of 1987 – not, by any metric, a vintage year for pop music. But Troy would have attracted attention at any point in history: a lyric in which WB Yeats gets bound up with the singer’s childhood trauma, a vocal so powerful it’s almost alarming, a high-drama string arrangement.

There are fine moments on O’Connor’s 00s albums Sean-Nós Nua, Throw Down Your Arms and Theology, but 2012’s How About I Be Me (and You Be You)? still felt like an all-guns-blazing return to form. The Wolf Is Getting Married packs a mighty chorus, its lyrics brimming with fresh optimism, and her voice sounds magnificent.

This is O’Connor at her don’t-mess fiercest, dismissing “all this man-trolling” – no to another husband, or indeed another boyfriend – over a churning alt-rock backing. There’s a faint hint of the Beatles about the tune; the hook is absolutely immense. How on earth was this not a huge hit?

Co-producer John Reynolds said O’Connor’s vocal on Fire on Babylon “possessed an energy that was almost impossible to contain”. Certainly, there’s a harrowing, red-raw quality to her singing on a track that revisits her abusive childhood and unflinchingly excoriates her mother. The reggae-infused backing sweetens the pill a little.

From the largely acoustic EP Gospel Oak – a very different beast indeed to its fraught predecessor, 1994’s Universal Mother – This Is to Mother You is just an extraordinarily beautiful, tender song. Subsequently covered by Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt, and reworked in 2009 as a charity duet with Mary J Blige, the original is still the keeper.

A one-off single that stalled just outside the UK Top 40, My Special Child was, perhaps, just too raw and personal in its treatment of the collapse of O’Connor’s marriage – and her decision to have an abortion – for mass consumption. There’s certainly nothing wrong with its stunning melody, nor its majestic and folky arrangement, though.

Co-written by Bono and produced by Bomb the Bass’s Tim Simenon, O’Connor’s contribution to the soundtrack for In the Name of the Father sets a folky melody and murder ballad-inspired lyric to a backdrop of pounding drums, ambient synths and distorted fiddle. Her voice sounds alternately flinty and agonised; the overall effect is stunning.

Despite its none-more-80s drums, O’Connor’s first hit sounded like nothing else in the charts on arrival. There’s a swaggering confidence about its faintly Clash-like guitar riff, its astonishing swooping vocal and its strange but intriguing words, complete with early statement of her unbiddable approach: “I have refused to take part.”

At first, it’s an exercise in restraint: nothing but an acoustic strum and O’Connor pouring out her heart about her divorce (the way she sings “I’ll talk but you won’t listen to me” is shattering ). Then, a minute before the end, the strumming gets more frantic and a sense of catharsis kicks in. An awesome song.

In a sense, it feels unfair putting Nothing Compares 2 U at the top of this list. It’s a cover, lording it over umpteen examples of O’Connor’s songwriting skill; moreover, it enjoyed the kind of vast, unrepeatable success that overshadows the rest of her oeuvre in the eyes of casual listeners. But then again … just listen to it. More than 35 years of familiarity haven’t done anything to dull its emotional impact: her voice whispers and soars, shifting from sorrow to anger to despair, completely inhabiting a lyric in which every suggestion to forget heartbreak and move forward falls on deaf ears. “It’s my song now,” she once remarked – tough talk when the author was Prince, but absolutely correct.

articles.title: The Thanksgiving food traditions we could all share
articles.summary: Warming pie, buttery mash and plenty of gravy are a perfect excuse to gather friends around the table during chilly November • Sign up here for our weekly food newsletter, Feast As a Brit, there are plenty of reasons for me not to embrace Thanksgiving, most of all because it isn’t actually a British holiday, and least of all because we already have quite enough occasions to eat ourselves silly between now and January. And yet, every November, as the days grow shorter and darker and colder, I find myself rather taken with the idea of hosting a seasonal dinner for friends. If Christmas is more formal and family-focused, then Thanksgiving feels like a prime opportunity to get pals around the table, eat until you need to undo your top trouser button, and take a moment to appreciate what you have. And if that means borrowing a few ideas from across the Atlantic – a warming spiced pumpkin pie , say, or a dish of fruity stuffing and a sharp cranberry sauce – well, there’s no reason we can’t make them our own. Obviously there are some crossovers with Britain’s main festive meal, turkey being the big one. Personally, I prefer to cook a cockerel on Christmas Day, which naturally gives me the opportunity to make turkey for Thanksgiving instead. Brining the bird in advance really is a gamechanger, and Margot Henderson’s buttermilk and harissa brine gives you the most succulent and aromatic meat. Rather than roasted, the potatoes are usually mashed and buttery, and if you are going to make that, then Joël Robuchon’s best mashed potatoes in the world are probably the way to go. Just remember, now is not the time to shy away from butter. Hetty McKinnon’s green bean tahini casserole recipe adds an injection of flavour and lightness to an otherwise rich meal, while Felicity Cloake’s perfect sweet potato casserole will undoubtedly be a key talking point – pecan praline and marshmallow topping for me, please. Warming pie, buttery mash and plenty of gravy are a perfect excuse to gather friends around the table during chilly November

A s a Brit, there are plenty of reasons for me not to embrace Thanksgiving, most of all because it isn’t actually a British holiday, and least of all because we already have quite enough occasions to eat ourselves silly between now and January. Obviously there are some crossovers with Britain’s main festive meal, turkey being the big one. Brining the bird in advance really is a gamechanger, and Margot Henderson’s buttermilk and harissa brine gives you the most succulent and aromatic meat. Rather than roasted, the potatoes are usually mashed and buttery, and if you are going to make that, then Joël Robuchon’s best mashed potatoes in the world are probably the way to go. Just remember, now is not the time to shy away from butter. Hetty McKinnon’s green bean tahini casserole recipe adds an injection of flavour and lightness to an otherwise rich meal, while Felicity Cloake’s perfect sweet potato casserole will undoubtedly be a key talking point – pecan praline and marshmallow topping for me, please.

Whether you call it Thanksgiving, an autumn celebration, or just an excuse to unite with friends on a miserable November Thursday, just make sure there’s enough gravy .

The great German Christmas bake off | One of my most loved and used Christmas cookbooks has been reissued with a new festive red cover. If baking is your thing, Anja Dunk’s book Advent is a must-have on your shelf. Filled with daily Christmas bakes inspired by her upbringing and German mother, plus striking lino prints made by Dunk herself, its reappearance every December is a source of immense joy.

P-p-pick up a pumpkin | My main reason for hosting a Thanksgiving-style dinner is wanting a reason to preorder Claire Ptak’s tequila pumpkin pie (although you really don’t need a formal reason). I appreciate that this is quite a London-centric recommendation, but fear not: the recipe also features in Claire’s book, Love is a Pink Cake , so everyone can get to enjoy it.

My new festive tipple | If, like me, you’re partial to a nightcap when the nights draw in, I highly recommend having a bottle of Welsh Barti cream liqueur in your cupboard. Elegant, warming with gentle spices and vanilla, it is the most glorious cream liqueur. Plus, it has a coconut base so is dairy-free, making it suitable for vegan guests, too. Serve over ice or in a warm, coffee-style cocktail.

articles.title: Wife of Trump ally Todd Blanche promoted treatments with unproven medical claims

articles.content:
Kristine Blanche, named to US health advisory role, offered purported treatments for Epstein-Barr virus and HPV

Attorney general Todd Blanche’s wife, Kristine Blanche, who was appointed earlier this year to a US government advisory board on alternative medicine, has a website on which she marketed dietary supplements and treatments with unproven medical and health claims.

Blanche is a licensed physician assistant who says she has a PhD in breast thermography from the University of Science, Arts and Technology in Montserrat, a British territory in the Caribbean. She is also an advocate for alternative medical cures and holistic health.

Her site also links to a page called “Dr Blanche’s Dispensary”, where patients can buy supplement pills she recommends. She suggested that one product, a liquid herbal compound, could be used to treat the Epstein-Barr virus, although she misspelled “Epstein”.

There is no medication approved by the FDA to treat or cure Epstein-Barr, and the product itself does not claim to treat the virus.

Blanche also listed five supplements in her store, priced up to $63 a bottle, which she said can help treat human papillomavirus (HPV).

Another treatment Blanche offers, priced online at $595, claims to help men “boost” their testosterone levels and lose weight.

The day after the Guardian emailed questions to Blanche about the supplements she offered, the products related to purported treatments for Epstein-Barr and HPV disappeared from her website. Her online store carries a disclaimer that “these statements have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration. These products are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.”

Peter Lurie, the executive director of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, said that Blanche’s website highlights gaps in regulations of claims made by providers. “That leaves an opening for some to exploit,” he said. “It is not in the interest of American patients, but it is not clearly illegal.”

Blanche wrote to the Guardian that she has “a PhD and an MD degree”, and said she complies “with all mandatory FDA guidelines. Any publication to the contrary is false and defamatory.”

She said that while she has a medical degree from the university in Montserrat, she has never been a licensed physician in the US. She has previously practiced as a physician assistant.

In April, Blanche was appointed to the advisory council of the federal National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH). The center, which has a $170m annual budget, supports research on alternative and holistic medicines and practices.

“It absolutely concerns me,” Lurie said of her appointment. “I have no confidence that the attorney general’s wife, with a financial interest in the kind of products this advisory committee concerns itself with, would be appropriate on the committee.”

In response to questions, a National Institutes of Health (NIH) spokesperson emailed that “the Trump administration is bringing the best and brightest into HHS”, adding: “Dr Kristine Blanche was appointed through the established appointment process based on her work and background in integrative health. Her experience provides a relevant foundation for service and a valuable perspective to inform the council’s work, in compliance with the charter.”

Iris International, which invests in medical companies, also hired Blanche this year as its chief medical officer. A spokesperson for the company wrote that Blanche “reports to the CEO and provides a view on emerging healthcare businesses in the market”.

It is unclear how much business Blanche does on her website, which appears to have been active for over a decade.

In Todd Blanche’s 2025 and 2026 financial disclosures, his wife’s income from “Integrative Healing Center” is not large, listed at just between $1,000 and $15,000.

Her “Man Up” cleanse and “Girlfriend” cleanse – each priced at almost $600 – are still available, and include detoxes, shakes, videos and dietary supplements.

“Lose weight, boost your testosterone & ditch the toxins. All while eating real food,” the Man Up program promises.

“I’m going to share with you how you can turn back your body into that place it was before. I’ve had patients lose 40 pounds,” Blanche said in a video sales pitch on YouTube. “It’s not acceptable to you if you’re not really feeling great.”

She has praised the use of a type of alternative diagnostic imaging technology called “thermography” – which detects heat variations in the body – and in a podcast has said it can predict potential risks years before mammograms. Her website says her PhD thesis was about “breast thermography”.

The FDA has approved the use of thermography if it is used with mammography, but has warned it cannot be a substitute.

The Blanches moved to Florida in 2024 and the website says she has a virtual practice in Palm Beach Gardens, where the couple live, not far from Mar-a-Lago. Her PA license lists her home address.

Last month, Blanche appeared on a little-watched podcast called I Choose Health, run by Stefan Lessie, a New York City-based personal trainer who posts inspirational and educational interviews with doctors and health activists.

Lessie has a tiny audience of about 20 to 30 listeners a week on Spotify. He said he received an unsolicited email last month from a PR executive explaining that “my client Kristine Blanche would resonate with your audience”.

Lessie interviewed Blanche for an hour , as she discussed her practice and her philosophy of medicine. “A lot of women come to me after they’ve been to many doctors over several years of suffering,” she told him.

“I love that the Maha movement is out there,” Blanche said, referring to Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again movement. “Trying to educate moms on, you know, food dyes are bad.”

Lessie said he did not know who Blanche was. “I was doing some research after the interview, and I saw her husband, and I was like: ‘He’s the US attorney general!’ And I was like, ‘Wow!’”

Blanche has received little, if any, public attention. A Stat News article in April reported her appointment to the federal advisory council.

The former head of the NCCIH, Dr Helene Langevin, a professor at the University of Vermont, said the advisory council role is “important” because members review every research grant decision made by independent panels.

Langevin, who retired in September 2025, declined to discuss specifics about Blanche. “I can’t comment on the qualifications of any advisory board member,” she said.

articles.title: Mauricio Pochettino calls for Manchester United to show no fear against Liverpool
articles.summary: New head coach’s first game is at Anfield on Sunday ‘We are going there with the idea to win and be brave’ Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield on Sunday for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start. United are 18th in the Premier League and Liverpool fourth but the head coach will not accept nerves. Pochettino is known for being attack-minded and will bring those ideals, but will have had only three days with the players since replacing Michael Carrick. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield on Sunday for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start.

United are 18th in the Premier League and Liverpool fourth but the head coach will not accept nerves. Pochettino is known for being attack-minded and will bring those ideals, but will have had only three days with the players since replacing Michael Carrick.

“We are going to go there to Anfield with the idea to win and be brave and to be Manchester United ,” Pochettino told the club’s website. “The history talks for us, and what we need to expect, and we are going to expect in Manchester United. We need to be sure that we are brave and we are protagonists and go there with no fears and challenge a very good team like Liverpool.”

Pochettino arrived in Manchester on Wednesday after an overnight flight, having taken charge of his final USA match against Haiti . He toured the training ground and held meetings with senior staff and players not on international duty. Members of Pochettino’s staff were in place earlier in the week as they seek to revitalise a team with one league win.

“We need to go little by little, step by step,” Pochettino said. “We cannot go too fast but also we need to, at the same time, attack the priorities to build something.”

He said it was important he and his staff adapt to the culture of the club. “And then, with this sense of knowing the history of the club, try to create all together, because we are all different, a culture, a philosophy that can respect that identity, the history of the club. But at the same time, performing. If we don’t perform, the responsibility is mine.”

Pochettino has coveted the United job and is a keen admirer of Sir Alex Ferguson, who he describes as “the best coach in history”. Since the Scot’s retirement in 2013, United have failed to match his success but Pochettino said he was looking at “the potential of the club”. The weight of past achievements has hindered individuals over the past 13 years.

“The players need to express their talent,” Pochettino said. “We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now: it’s to work with them and try to take the pressure.

“Pressure needs to bring energy, responsibility needs to bring energy. Because if not, it’s too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back. When you connect with the game, you connect through your talent when you feel freedom, when you feel happy, when you want to play for your teammates, when you want to play for your family, when you want to play for your club, your fans.”

He sounded an upbeat note, saying: “With the power of this club and the fans supporting us, I think we will get in the place that we deserve to be.”

United’s total borrowings have risen to £784.5m, with long-term debt up by almost £100m over the past year. Figures published for the three months to 30 September show long-term borrowings of £577.4m, compared with £481.2m 12 months earlier. United’s cash reserves fell from £80.5m to £55.5m over the same period despite an increase in revenue.

The club reported a quarterly ⁠net loss of £18.1m, compared with £6.6m ​in ​the same period a year earlier. Revenue rose by 4% to £146m.

articles.title: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden

articles.content:
The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly

I t’s injury time at the Emirates on the 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Spurs. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and on to the post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs fans before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it.

But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport . As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”.

It’s just a noise, but it’s unmistakingly Danny Kelly. He regains the power of speech and follows it up with: “Gooooaaaal … Goalll Stan Goalll at the Emirates.” Reporter Ian Abrahams and Stan Collymore join the excitement, before Danny comes back: “I LOVE FOOTBALL, STAN, I LOVE IT.” It is such a brilliant piece of radio . From one of the absolute greats.

Danny died last week. In a beautiful tribute on the Spurs podcast he hosted – A View From The Lane – Charlie Eccleshare pointed out the irony that for someone so articulate and erudite and able to do so much more than just “the football”, his most iconic moment is so simple. Even the opening noise – not even a real word – is perfect in that context.

Words such as pioneer and trailblazer often get thrown out in moments like this. But Danny really was. I first met him at BBC London more than 20 years ago. As someone who’d listened to him and Danny Baker as a teenager, I couldn’t really believe I was in the same office as them.

His career was ridiculous, editing the NME and Q magazine, setting up Football365, but it was radio where I knew him. He understood the absurdity of life and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living by talking about football.

I remember at TalkSport one World Cup – 2018 perhaps – wandering in and he was hosting a live match, watching a game on the TV just marvelling at the fact that this was a job, and that this was his job.

And he was funny. Blimey he was funny – what an ability to be blessed with. I listened to a best of Baker and Kelly Upfront from the old Radio 5 on YouTube the other day; amazing calls about Arthur Cox locking a disgruntled fan in his office for two and a half hours, a man playing football with a pig’s head in a sausage factory in Peckham: “I used to like the volleys when the eyes used to pop out.” Anyone who has tried to make funny football content, of any kind – radio, TV, podcasts, social media – owes a debt of gratitude to him.

Last Wednesday afternoon Charlie Baker and I had to try to do him justice on TalkSport. Afternoon UK time, midnight til 3am for me in Australia. I was asleep when my phone rang and instantly presumed I’d slept through my alarm and missed the show. A millisecond of internal panic surged through me as I jumped up and cracked a shin on the bedside table. Danny would appreciate the ridiculous scene of me hopping around in the dark trying not to wake the kids while one of the bosses gave me the incredibly sad news.

If you’ve broadcast for any amount of time, you will be confronted with having to host shows just after someone has died. Jack Charlton, Terry Venables, Jimmy Greaves – but never before have I had to pay tribute to a friend.

Paul Hawksbee’s voice cracks and we all go. There are West Ham and Chelsea fans calling admitting they listen to his Spurs podcast because it’s him. There are all manner of texts recounting hilarious stories they heard on his shows over the last 30 years: the man who took a TV to a game in Northern Ireland so they could watch the FA Cup final, having to move around holding the aerial to keep the signal.

There’s a moment I think Danny would have found so funny, when I’m being sad – because it is sad, and I am sad – and into the break I read the sponsor’s lines: “This show is brought to you by Toolstation, first stop Toolstation” in such a maudlin way it’s as if I’m delivering a eulogy, just one sponsored by a hardware store. I catch myself just in time.

But most importantly there are so many messages from people who never met Danny, who never knew him, but who felt as if they knew him. We believed he would have wanted a bit of fuss made of him.

He definitely knew the enduring power of radio, even as the broadcasting landscape changes so quickly. It connects in a way nothing else can. And nothing said that more than messages we received from listeners who at one time or another were struggling and going through incredibly hard times and Danny’s energy, wit and joy were an escape and a tonic.

There will be a million people more important in Danny’s life than me. Our paths crossed a great deal, but never for very long. I was a minuscule cog in his world – but Danny had so much love to give. Voice notes about how to broadcast remotely or celebrating Spurs’ win in Bilbao; the tributes showed he had almost infinite time for others.

It always feels such a bland cliche to say it’s impossible to consider someone so full of life not being there – we all know that we have a sell-by date. At the start of October he had been given a choice: to ebb away slowly over a couple of years or have a big but very risky operation. Danny never ebbed.

He sent a big group WhatsApp voice note to many friends and colleagues, and I don’t think he would mind me writing what it said.

“I want you to know that I’ve enjoyed being around you, I’ve learnt from you, I’ve enjoyed working with you, you know how much I love my work – the fact I’m pretty good at it is secondary to how much I enjoy it, but look I’m very much hopeful that the boffins and my own determination will get me through this and we can all laugh about this message. But know how I care about you, how much you have meant in my life and on Thursday night or Friday morning when you look at the sky or feel the wind against your face, think about me and what’s happening and hopefully we’ll all have a pint and a laugh about this somewhere down the line.”

From “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH” to that – his words just hit the right tone every time.

I listened to a best of Baker and Kelly Upfront from the old Radio 5 on YouTube the other day; amazing calls about Arthur Cox locking a disgruntled fan in his office for two and a half hours, a man playing football with a pig’s head in a sausage factory in Peckham: “I used to like the volleys when the eyes used to pop out.” Anyone who has tried to make funny football content, of any kind – radio, TV, podcasts, social media – owes a debt of gratitude to him.

Last Wednesday afternoon Charlie Baker and I had to try to do him justice on TalkSport. Afternoon UK time, midnight til 3am for me in Australia. I was asleep when my phone rang and instantly presumed I’d slept through my alarm and missed the show. A millisecond of internal panic surged through me as I jumped up and cracked a shin on the bedside table. Danny would appreciate the ridiculous scene of me hopping around in the dark trying not to wake the kids while one of the bosses gave me the incredibly sad news.

If you’ve broadcast for any amount of time, you will be confronted with having to host shows just after someone has died. Jack Charlton, Terry Venables, Jimmy Greaves – but never before have I had to pay tribute to a friend.

Paul Hawksbee’s voice cracks and we all go. There are West Ham and Chelsea fans calling admitting they listen to his Spurs podcast because it’s him. There are all manner of texts recounting hilarious stories they heard on his shows over the last 30 years: the man who took a TV to a game in Northern Ireland so they could watch the FA Cup final, having to move around holding the aerial to keep the signal.

There’s a moment I think Danny would have found so funny, when I’m being sad – because it is sad, and I am sad – and into the break I read the sponsor’s lines: “This show is brought to you by Toolstation, first stop Toolstation” in such a maudlin way it’s as if I’m delivering a eulogy, just one sponsored by a hardware store. I catch myself just in time.
But most importantly there are so many messages from people who never met Danny, who never knew him, but who felt as if they knew him. We believed he would have wanted a bit of fuss made of him.

He definitely knew the enduring power of radio, even as the broadcasting landscape changes so quickly. It connects in a way nothing else can. And nothing said that more than messages we received from listeners who at one time or another were struggling and going through incredibly hard times and Danny’s energy, wit and joy were an escape and a tonic.

There will be a million people more important in Danny’s life than me. Our paths crossed a great deal, but never for very long. I was a minuscule cog in his world – but Danny had so much love to give. Voice notes about how to broadcast remotely or celebrating Spurs’ win in Bilbao; the tributes showed he had almost infinite time for others.

It always feels such a bland cliche to say it’s impossible to consider someone so full of life not being there – we all know that we have a sell-by date. At the start of October he had been given a choice: to ebb away slowly over a couple of years or have a big but very risky operation. Danny never ebbed.
He sent a big group WhatsApp voice note to many friends and colleagues, and I don’t think he would mind me writing what it said.

“I want you to know that I’ve enjoyed being around you, I’ve learnt from you, I’ve enjoyed working with you, you know how much I love my work – the fact I’m pretty good at it is secondary to how much I enjoy it, but look I’m very much hopeful that the boffins and my own determination will get me through this and we can all laugh about this message. But know how I care about you, how much you have meant in my life and on Thursday night or Friday morning when you look at the sky or feel the wind against your face, think about me and what’s happening and hopefully we’ll all have a pint and a laugh about this somewhere down the line.”
From “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH” to that – his words just hit the right tone every time.

articles.title: UK joins in GTA 6 frenzy as game becomes available worldwide
articles.summary: The game, which was in development for 13 years, is set become one of the world's most popular entertainment products ever.
articles.content:
After years of anticipation and delays, as well as controversy around worker rights, Grand Theft Auto 6 has completed its phased worldwide release and is available to gamers everywhere, including the UK.

There has been near universal praise from critics, with review aggregator Metacritic calculating its average score at 99 out of 100 based on 150 reviews. , external

Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has held the top spot since 1998 - but Metacritic confirmed to the BBC that this has now officially been overtaken.

GTA 6 is set to become one of the world's most popular entertainment products ever, with fans booking time off work, and schools warning students not to bunk off.

Some schools have reminded parents and pupils to prioritise study over the game, which has an 18 rating , external for "strong graphic violence, strong sexual themes and use of illegal drugs".

One school in Essex incentivised pupils to attend with prize s such as vouchers, Christmas dinners and a pass to skip the lunch queue.

The UK rating means it can only be legally sold to an adult. It does not stop an adult letting their child play the game - instead it is meant to inform their decision.

It's the game that shocked and thrilled the world: Grand Theft Auto. As a new installment is released in 2026, go deep into the history of the game with rapper Bugzy Malone.

The game, set in the fictional US state of Leonida, follows two protagonists, Lucia and Jason, through the seedy underbelly of America after an "easy score goes wrong".

It was released at midnight in all the countries it is available in, which meant New Zealanders were the first to access it.

"The graphics are great. Even from the set-up and credits, it's feeling pretty good," Aleana Fernando, who lives in Auckland, New Zealand, told BBC Newsbeat soon after she started playing.

Once the game was released at midnight UK time, gamers were equally enthralled by the game's graphics and attention to detail.

Charlie Wood from London said he had "already laughed at the dialogue before even stepping into the gameplay".

About 30 minutes into playing in Leonida, he said it was "most definitely worth the wait".

The Guardian's Keza MacDonald , external was impressed by the relationship between the main characters.

"GTA has never been particularly kind to women... there is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI's world, but now we have Lucia to react to it," she said.

"This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story".

After GTA 5 became one of the most successful entertainment products of all time - with estimates of net profits soaring as high up as $10bn (£7.6bn) - anticipation could not be higher for the sixth instalment.

Makers Rockstar North, headquartered in Edinburgh, delayed the release twice, saying it needed extra months to finish the game with the level of polish fans had come to "expect and deserve".

The company was also set back by hacks and leaks of its unfinished version.

On Monday, 21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, pleaded guilty to the Rockstar Games hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.

He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished and hugely anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.

A group of Rockstar workers who were sacked by the company have also been protesting outside its offices, ahead of a tribunal which heard they were penalised for discussing working conditions in a private online forum while working on the game.

They claimed they were punished for being part of a workers' union, but Thomas Cordrey, representing Rockstar, said employees made disparaging comments about the company on a semi-public Discord server and shared confidential information.

Tech Now's Laura Cress previews GTA 6 with the game's original creators

Players were able to download the 212GB game ahead of time, in order to be able to play it as soon as it was made available.

Some had even gone to the lengths of buying a whole new console dedicated to the game.

Broadband providers Virgin Media O2, as well as BT and EE, said internet traffic records had been broken in the days leading up to the UK release.

The BBC has heard from people planning to take time off work - as well as a company which has given its employees the day off - in order to dedicate time to the game.

Kieran Youens-Byrne, 34, from Manchester said he was "going on a pilgrimage to Wales" where he would be "completely off grid" for a week.

He added his partner Clare "has been incredibly understanding, although I suspect she's questioning why our romantic getaway revolves around a PlayStation".

Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6

Grand Theft Auto staff sacked as 'shock tactic' to punish trade union activity, tribunal hears

articles.title: Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’

articles.content:
Spain Under-21 striker admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he must stay calm over goal drought at Fulham

T he first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under-21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one.

Time to talk, so let’s start with tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. His great-aunt, born Margarita Carmen Cansino, was among the biggest stars in Hollywood, although he’s not sure he’s seen any of her films. His grandfather was a surgeon and others in the family followed. His uncles played rugby for Spain, but that wasn’t his thing. As for him, he enrolled in a degree in business management and analytics, and reckons he might have liked law, yet even that wasn’t his chosen field.

Hayworth’s family was from Seville province. “I know she was a great actress but I’m afraid I have to admit I’m not one for old films,” García concedes in an even tone. “My uncles played rugby for Ciencias and practically all of them were in the national team together. They tried to get me to play with my cousins, but I was always more into football.” He was good at it too: another Spain international, the Club World Cup’s top scorer, playing for Real Madrid .

Then this summer, with opportunities limited, he joined Fulham, his introductory interview conducted in impeccable English . Having joined Madrid aged 10, he was leaving home for the first time, as Fulham’s record signing, at 22. He had the language and intelligence to embrace it. As for being uprooted, he was used to that, growing up in Argentina and Chile as well as Spain.

“From very little my parents impressed upon me the importance of study, learning languages,” García says. “I’m at Villanueva university [in Madrid]. I started with dual honours business and analytics although that became difficult with my profession. Now it’s just business, and I’m trying to arrange with the university how best to handle it [from London]. My parents considered it fundamental to speak English and I was always at international schools.

“Every two or three years we would change city. Obviously, there would be phases when I felt: ‘ Pfff, again?!’ Having to move home because of my parents’ work. But I look back and feel grateful because, seen with perspective, it gives you opportunities to meet new people, see new places, learn. I’ve always had foreign friends with whom I spoke English.”

García has been joined at Fulham by César Palacios and Manuel Ángel from Madrid’s academy. Three 22-year-olds, like your very own Erasmus course. “Nah,” García says, laughing. “I wouldn’t call it an Erasmus because we’re talking about a big, ambitious career step. We’re grateful for the trust placed in us. I’ve been pleasantly surprised by London, a huge city with people from all nationalities and cultures and Fulham fit the situation I was in, the desire to grow.

“Álvaro Arbeloa explained the project, convinced me. I’d worked with him in Madrid. He knows me perfectly, how far he can push me. Equally, I know what he wants of me. That helps … [Arbeloa] told me it was a project that it will take time but that he needed me. I’m very, very happy. It’s one of the world’s best leagues, if not the best.”

And the toughest? Is English football as wild as it looks? “Yes!” García replies. “They had told me it was demanding, hard, but …” He cracks up. “I have to admit it still surprised me. That first game against Chelsea , I finished really, really tired. It was box to box, intense, a lot of running. Bit by bit I’m adapting. The intensity and pace is very different.

“Spain is more tactical, a bit more technical. English football is pace. You can’t lose concentration for a second, not a second. Anything can happen any moment. How many Premier League games are decided late? Suddenly there’s a goal in the 90th minute and again on 93. It’s your corner and their chance. The level of concentration, that constant transition, is what most sets the Premier League apart.”

Despite defeat on that opening day against Chelsea, García scored. A superb goal followed against AFC Wimbledon in the Carabao Cup . “It was super special to do it at Craven Cottage – I love how close the fans are; they can reach out and touch you. But I don’t consider myself someone who’s easily satisfied. I’m not like that. I always want more, more, more.”

García hasn’t scored since and Fulham went five league games without a win, pressure building. Which is where the calmness comes in. By the time they faced Hull, Arbeloa appeared on the edge of the sack, questions asked about his signings, García especially. Were three Madrid academy kids really what Fulham needed? Was the coach’s relationship with them not such a good thing after all?

No player is impermeable to what is said, García admits, but he insists: “We treat that as outside noise. And we all knew that the beginning wouldn’t be easy. There’s a change of cycle: the coach goes, a new coach comes, there are signings, a different system, idea. Everyone has to adapt: those already at the club and those of us who are new. We’re young too. Results weren’t going our way but we had good intentions: to play good football, build, apply the manager’s ideas bit by bit. We had to remain calm.”

Fulham go into Saturday’s game at Manchester City unbeaten in four in the league, the sense of them shifting towards something more pragmatic not shared by García. “I don’t think we changed anything against Hull,” he says of a game Fulham won 1-0 . “We didn’t do anything we weren’t already doing. Nothing. Maybe we controlled the small details that hurt us but the idea was the same. The players were very clear what the manager asked, very firm: it was just a question of time. You have to be patient. If you watch Fulham, you see the manager’s idea: have the ball, construct attacks well, show maximum intensity constantly with and without the ball. Aggressive, ambitious.”

Chances are coming for García but goals aren’t. He has started every league game but not scored or assisted since the opening day. Yet if there is a sense of a man feeling the pressure, that’s not repeated here; instead there’s an evenness, an ease. And a smile when another, more welcome, stat is raised: he has made more off-the-ball runs into the area than anyone. Something to hold on to, perhaps, a process that will pay off. “Really?” he says. “Well, I’m happy for people to see that a striker can help the team without the ball. In the end, it’s about following the manager’s instructions.”

In the end though, teams will be judged on results and strikers on goals, price too. He knows: this is what he does, the path he chose. “Pressure depends on how you look at it, really,” García says. “Football is [very psychological]. It happens fast: it doesn’t give you time to enjoy good moments or linger on bad ones. It’s a rollercoaster: up there, down here. It’s not flat, but you maintain balance, work daily, improve: go in, focus, repeat.

“It’s not that I don’t ‘care’ about the price, it’s that the market is the market; it doesn’t depend on me. Calmness always, perspective … I know strikers are measured by goals but, well, the days I don’t score I’m completely sure I will be able to walk off the pitch and say that, no matter what happened, I helped my team, doing a load of other things. It is what it is.”

It is also time. A head peers around the door, the bus is going. García holds out a hand, apologises again. “It’s been a pleasure,” he says.

articles.content:
There’s a vast amount to absorb in Leonida, but these pointers will rev up your criminal engines and allow you to better enjoy the ride

Leonida is so huge as to be overwhelming and in the opening hours, the game bombards you with tonnes of info that you will inevitably forget. But I’ve done nothing but play this game for weeks and I’m here to help. Here’s what I wished I’d known at the start

Walk faster. I found that Jason and Lucia walk incredibly slowly. If you go into the options menu, you can select “fast walk” as the default walking speed, which sped them up just a little without ruining the pace or atmosphere of the game. While you’re in there, you can also customise plenty of other things, including controls and button mapping.

Don’t worry too much about money. In the opening chapters of the game – which could take you 20 or more hours to play through – it can feel like everything is expensive and there’s never enough cash. But later on, you will have many more ways to make money and a $200 cab ride will feel like nothing. This problem will fix itself, so in the meantime, just enjoy yourself.

Bank your cash at ATMs. If you get busted by the cops or killed by anyone, you will lose a lot of your cash – and anything you had in your stash bags, too. Trouble can start at any time in Vice City, so it’s not a great idea to walk around with holdalls full of drugs and pockets full of money. Use the BuckMe app on your phone to find your nearest ATM and bank your cash, so it remains safe. And you can stash those holdalls in the trunk of your car.

Do not use your own vehicle for anything illegal . If your car is hanging around near a crime scene and the cops identify it, it’ll get impounded, which is a massive pain because you have to steal it back. Instead, just hotwire a getaway car and have it parked nearby. Then you can abandon it later with impunity.

Get your partner to fence your goods. If you cannot be bothered to drive all the way to a fence, you can hand your stash bags to your partner and ask them to do it before returning to you. You might get a little less money this way, but it saves repetitive drives and conversations. Later in the game you can also ask your fences to pick stuff up from stash boxes in your owned garages.

During missions, make liberal use of the “retry from checkpoint” option. Outside of story missions, you have to deal with the consequences of your blunders in GTA VI, whether you miss your highway exit on a long drive, pull out a gun at the wrong moment in a restaurant and start a mini gang war, or mess up a robbery and get busted. But inside the missions? You can neatly erase all your problems by pausing the game and selecting “retry checkpoint”. Take a wrong turn? Retry checkpoint. Shot the wrong person? Retry checkpoint. Accidentally run someone over? Retry checkpoint. Ended up miles from where you’re supposed to be after escaping the cops? Retry checkpoint, it usually gets you closer. This saved me a lot of time and frustration, and there was still quite enough unpredictable chaos and self-inflicted disaster to deal with outside of the story missions.

Don’t kill anyone unless you have to. Surprisingly you can get a lot of crime done in GTA VI without doing much killing at all (outside of story missions where you have to shoot a zillion bad guys/pursuing cops). On robberies and stick-ups you’re rewarded for stealth. You can sometimes sneak in unnoticed through back doors and avoid security entirely. But if that’s not an option – if a security guard starts shooting instead of surrendering when you point a gun at them, for instance – then non-lethal solutions attract less trouble from the cops. You can shoot an arm or leg to disable someone rather than killing them, or knock them out with the butt of a gun. All of this will make your getaway easier and make you feel less guilty.

Understand how heat works. Crime is a little more complex in GTA VI. Your wanted level is still indicated by stars, and this is directly related to the seriousness of your crime. Stealing a car is one star, robbing a store is three or more, killing cops always adds another star. The police response escalates with your wanted level, determining whether they send out helicopters or set up roadblocks to stop you. But now there’s also “heat”: in areas where you’ve previously committed a crime, the cops will be looking for you. They’ll have a description of your car and your outfit. A simple thing you can do is always put on a mask and a hat before you do anything that might attract the cops – then you can simply remove them afterwards. It’s also wise to change vehicles once you’re out of sight of witnesses and police. Changing outfits is more difficult: you have to store them in the trunk of your own car or buy new ones – but I found that changing cars and wearing masks was usually enough.

Watch your criminal profile. GTA VI tracks your actions as both Jason and Lucia and gives them a criminal profile. Unnecessary violence such as running people over or shooting bystanders will quickly turn you from “professional” or “hardened” to “violent” or “psycho”, which has serious repercussions for the game’s story and ending. If you go too far then either character can become “irredeemable”, and there’s no way back. You can get your criminal profile back into the professional range by being as non-lethal as possible and leaving innocent bystanders alone.

Expect people to fight back . This is Leonida: pedestrians are often packing. If you start behaving badly or insulting people on the street, someone might throw a punch or pull a gun on you. Drive into someone’s car and they might have an episode of road rage and spent the next few minutes chasing you down and trying to run you off the road. This is all extremely fun – insulting people on the street sometimes leads to some hilarious back-and-forth exchanges – but if you’re trying to stay out of trouble, don’t mess with the locals.

Prepare for big thefts . You can get away with a simple liquor store smash’n’grab by running in, waving your gun about and then getting outta there, but later in the game, if you want to rob anywhere with a real return – a bank, or a big jewellery store – then you need to have a plan for when the police inevitably turn up. Park your car somewhere quiet and fill the trunk with a change of clothes, so that you can return to it after the job, stash your loot and weapons in the trunk, and disguise yourself. If you’re clever with this you can walk or drive right past the cops after a job, safe in the knowledge that you won’t be recognised. Parking your own car in a parking garage is an especially clever option, as helicopters can’t see you in there.

Rob the criminals instead. I wasn’t far into this game before I started to feel bad about terrorising small business owners for money, but you don’t technically have to do much of this. You can make just as much money by robbing other criminals. Leonida is full of gang hangouts that you can easily infiltrate, full of drugs and cash that you can steal. The risk is that gang members will shoot you on sight if they see you skulking about, but helpfully, that also makes me feel less bad about shooting back.

Know when to cut your losses. Whether you’re robbing a store or trying to steal cocaine from under the noses of terrifying biker gangs, things can go south very fast in GTA. Sometimes the best idea is just to get outta thereand avoid losing whatever you’ve gained.

Sometimes it’s easier to get away on foot. If the cops are really chasing you down, with armoured cars and helicopters, it can be very difficult to get away in a car. Sometimes the best thing you can do is get out and run away on foot, making use of alleyways and covered parking garages in the city and tree cover out in the countryside. I once spent a good 15 minutes failing to get away from the police on the highway, crashing three cars in the process, before diving into a river and swimming desperately to the other side, ending up hiding on a golf course with $100k in stolen bills.

Take your time. This truly is an extraordinarily massive game and it will take weeks to get through even if you play for several hours a day. If you’re enjoying yourself, don’t feel like you have to rush to make progress. I found every chapter of this game to be enjoyable in its own way, and they all feel different from each other. We’ve been waiting a long time for this game – why not linger?

articles.title: You be the judge: should my friend stop eating smelly meals at work?
articles.summary: Mina’s substantial, aromatic workplace breakfasts and lunches are a concern for her friend and colleague Jackie. You decide who’s making a meal of the situation • Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a juror I recommended Mina as an intern but now worry as she’s always eating pungent food at her desk Who says you can only eat simple meals in the office? It’s fun to be creative with food Continue reading...
articles.content:
Mina’s substantial, aromatic workplace breakfasts and lunches are a concern for her friend and colleague Jackie. You decide who’s making a meal of the situation

I recommended Mina as an intern but now worry as she’s always eating pungent food at her desk

Mina and I have known each other since university and now we both work at the same company – she is on an internship that I helped her get. I have just completed mine and now work there part-time. It’s a nice company and it’s fun to see a friendly face in the office.

My only gripe is Mina’s office breakfasts and lunches. I feel second-hand embarrassment for her sometimes because she insists on bringing in elaborate meats and cheeses that she eats at her desk. She should be able to eat what she wants, but when I was an intern I’d eat breakfast at home and then have something quick at my desk for lunch.

I think it’s important to make a good impression, and to not stand in the kitchen putting together a complicated meal at nine in the morning. But Mina doesn’t care. She is obsessed with hitting her protein goals and says: “I need to eat this now!” I think there are other ways of hitting your goals.

Mina will have hoisin duck with pancakes or a honey-glazed salmon with spinach for breakfast. I can smell her meal in the office as I walk to my desk first thing in the morning. I think she should be a bit more conscious of the aromas her food is bringing into the office early in the morning, and how long she spends eating at her desk.

She rarely pops out to eat with the team. I know from experience that managers assess behaviour as well as competency, and I want her to get a permanent role. It’s about how well you get on with the company culture and no one else eats like she does.

There’s such a thing as trying to fit in when you’re on probation or starting out. I’m not aware of anyone saying anything negative about her, but I want to protect her reputation as well as my own, because I recommended her. Maybe I’m just overthinking it because I really care about what others think – clearly more than Mina does at least – and I don’t think you should make yourself stand out for your food choices in a new job.

Who says you can only eat simple meals in the office? It’s fun to be creative with food

I’m vehemently against western breakfast ideals. Who says that you can only eat fruit and yoghurt for breakfast? I much prefer to have a whole duck leg or half a chicken in the morning to ensure I hit my protein goals, then the same again at lunch.

It’s fun to be creative with what I eat, and I don’t think being an intern should mean that I compromise on that. Also, I think Jackie needs to be careful with the comment about the smell of my food because I’m not white. These days telling ethnic minorities that their food stinks could result in a tribunal.

I know we’re mates and she’s looking out for me, but I’ve had good appraisals so far and no one else seems to mind. I don’t know if she feels partly responsible for me as she brought me in, but if I’m not kept on, it won’t reflect badly on her. It’s between me and our boss.

The smell issue is funny because everyone’s food smells. If someone makes porridge and cinnamon, that smells. Coffee smells. Someone’s leftover curry smells. We all have to share a workplace with other people, and that means encountering things we wouldn’t personally choose. The notion that there’s a hierarchy of smells – or that fish can only be microwaved after 1pm – is archaic.

Unless my breakfast is genuinely making people uncomfortable or disrupting their work, I don’t think it’s reasonable to expect me to change my routine. Lots of people also eat breakfast and lunch at their desks, so I’m not an anomaly. I don’t go out for lunch with colleagues much because I can’t afford it.

Jackie seems to think that when you’re an intern, you should keep your head down and avoid attention. I think doing good work and treating colleagues well are more important.

Just because Jackie wouldn’t eat duck for breakfast doesn’t mean it’s wrong. And if that’s the only thing our company has to say about me, I think my professional reputation is just fine.

Jackie, wind your neck in, kiddo! If there’s an issue in the workplace, then Mina’s manager will handle it. This is 2026 – if people have an issue with food smells, that’s not a work culture you want to be in. Manisha, 53

It might be wise of Mina to be aware of the smells of her food. No one has complained, but maybe they won’t because of the reason she has stated. But Jackie should realise that nobody is judging her for this situation, and that it’s not her business. Bonnie, 71

It sounds like Mina has her life sorted: hitting nutrition goals, eating nice food and sticking to her budget. She certainly shouldn’t let the corporate grind guilt-trip her into the Pret queue. Ananya, 29

Mina should be judged on her work, not her diet. However, shared workspaces require consideration, and while there’s no “smell hierarchy,” certain foods smell strong regardless of origin. So if you have a communal area, maybe enjoy them there rather than at your desk. Michael, 29

I’m still mortified by the time I was told off for eating lasagne at my desk as a fashion intern 10 years ago, so I understand Jackie’s concern. It seems that everyone is happy with Mina’s work so far, however. Eat those duck legs to your heart’s content! Rebecca, 32

In our online poll, tell us: is Mina quackers for preferring roast duck to a bowl of cereal for breakfast?

We asked whether Maddie should stop calling sister when she’s on the move.
