articles.content:
When hibernation season hits, it’s time to turn up the cozy. These comforting picks, including soft PJs, fluffy neck warmers and festive candles, will help

The best personalized gift ideas, from a timeless tote bag to custom stationery

I try to keep my home looking and feeling nice all through the year, but once cold weather arrives, the cozy factor gets cranked to the max. I’m talking chicken soup bubbling on the stove, spicy-scented candles flickering, and a puzzle always in progress on the coffee table. It is my opinion that a cozy atmosphere should be profoundly comfortable and a bit nostalgic, cozy clothing should be soft and roomy, and cozy decor should be downright adorable.

If you know a person who lives to be cozy (or you are this person), I have rounded up some gift ideas that are sure to please during the holiday season and beyond.

Visit our ultimate holiday gift guide for more gift guides and holiday shopping ideas for everyone on your list.

A hot beverage is a must in chilly weather. But as someone who takes hours to finish just one cup of coffee, I have to get up several times to revive my lukewarm drink in the microwave – at least, that’s how it used to be before I bought this superb mug warmer for my desk. I just plug it in, set it to 150F for two hours, and my cup of coffee is kept steaming like a little geyser for as long as it takes for me to finish it. For an elevated version that heats an included mug through induction, Filter commissioning editor Karen Yuan loves her Ohom Ui .

Making the house smell nice has become increasingly important to me – particularly after a friend walked in and remarked that our home smelled like chili, despite us not having cooked chili in recent memory. It was a scarring event that led to keeping a constant rotation of scented candles on our entryway table. This time of year, I like the cinnamon-spice atmosphere that the Harvest Yankee Candle provides. It burns cleanly and evenly, casting a warm flickering light by our front door. For those seeking a scentless option, these flameless color-changing candles also provide the desired ambience.

Truthfully, I am smitten with just about everything from Rifle Paper Co, just for how well they do cozy. Case in point: this soft fleece blanket that is my constant companion when the temperature drops. It’s instantly warming, and the folksy, colorful pattern is delightful. Measuring 80 x 50in, it keeps me covered when I sprawl out on the couch – and is even roomy enough to share with a movie-watching buddy, if you’re feeling generous.

Piecing together a puzzle is my preferred method of easing into the morning and winding down at night. I have a large collection to choose from, but some of my favorites by far are from Magic Puzzle Company. I am drawn in by the quirky, colorful designs and wacky-shaped pieces. Plus, there is always a twist once you have completed the final step (I won’t say more than this). It’s a great gift for kids and adults alike, and one you can do with them. Get the fireplace going, play some moody music and get puzzling.

Achieving coziness requires warmth (the feeling and aesthetic). This Royal Robbins sweater fits the bill. Knitted with organic cotton blended with merino wool, it’s a dreamy combination of soft, warm and breathable, perfect for holiday parties or casual hangouts. I freely borrow it from my husband from time to time, so this cozy sweater just may become a cold-weather favorite for your giftee and their partner.

Advent calendars are such a fun tradition – who doesn’t love daily gifts ? – and a hot drink on a chilly morning is the coziest way to start the day. This Fresh Roasted Coffee Advent Calendar contains 24 single-serving pods with holiday flavors, artisan and dark roast blends, and single origin coffees inside. A shameless caffeine fiend, I opened mine early. I’ve been savoring the routine of peeling back the little door to a new flavor, such as Warm Gingerbread or Salted Caramel Mocha, and inhaling the delicious aroma of fresh coffee burbling into my mug.

Though they don’t get nearly enough love as holiday gifts, warm socks are a fantastic present and an important part of a cozy getup. Made with organic cotton, these socks from the Landmark Project have modest arch support plus a reinforced toe and heel for a perfect fit and extra durability. I like the cheery Prismatic pattern, while my husband prefers the south-western vibe and earth tones of the Western Fade pair. They’re a fun addition to any outfit and most importantly keep my feet nice and toasty.

I can’t change into PJs quickly enough once it gets dark out and work is done for the day. These buttery soft pajamas from the Company Store were made for relaxation, and the festive holiday pattern gives me that nostalgic “kid on Christmas morning” feeling. They come in several other fun designs, so you can get matching pairs for the whole family.

I used to buy new slippers annually – mostly the cheap department store variety, which are often shapeless and wear out within a year. These slip-ons from Glerups have officially ended that cycle. Made of 100% natural wool, they are moisture-wicking and odor-free, delightfully warm, and fit like a glove (after a few wears, they become molded to the shape of your foot). I chose the natural rubber outsole for extra traction on hardwood floors, but you also can’t go wrong with a soft, flexible leather sole . I rarely walk around the house without them, and after three years of regular use, they’re still in excellent condition.

Delightfully baggy and stretchy, this oversized onesie is a year-round staple for me – I got it in two colors so I can wear it as often as possible. In warm weather I pair it with a tank top, but in the cold months I add a long-sleeve shirt, throw on a jacket or cardigan , and bask in the feeling of achieving peak coziness. It’s an excellent gift for a friend who loves to travel, ramble around town or hunker down for movie nights.

Turtle Fur’s luxuriously soft and fluffy Single Layer Neck Warmer is my new go-to scarf alternative. It envelopes my neck and chin in warmth, and I love not having to deal with extra lengths of fabric dangling over my coat. Made of 100% recycled high-pile fleece, it’s as soft as cotton candy and will keep your recipient cozy whether they are on the chairlift or out for a walk on a chilly day.

When the days get shorter and colder, I find myself spending more time indoors, often curled up with a book. This beautifully embroidered journal – which comes with two cute little bonus bookmarks – allows me to log each book that I read. It encourages deeper reflection with writing prompts including “my favorite parts”, “questions” and “lessons and takeaways”. For maximum coziness and whimsy , I highly recommend using these smooth-writing carrot pens to jot down all bookish thoughts, ideally by candlelight.

Other gift ideas you might enjoy from the Filter , the Guardian’s guide to buying fewer, better things:

Gift ideas for the person who already has everything and the person who is always a bit cold

articles.title: Alice Zaslavsky’s recipe for cheesy greens with pastry sailboats

articles.content:
A speedy, weeknight riff on mkhlovani – Georgia’s version of spanakopita – skips the fiddly stuffing and long bake time, using store-bought puff pastry instead

Mkhlovani is Georgia’s answer to spanakopita, where wild greens, or the tops of hardy veg such as beets, are sauteed and stuffed into a dough.

But baking stuffed things midweek means too much waiting around, so I’m dividing and conquering, baking crunchy “sails” of shop-bought puff pastry while the greens schvitz in the pan.

When you buy beetroot, remember to stash the washed leaves in the freezer for this dish. You can also use greens such as silverbeet, chard, cavolo nero leaves or English spinach.

Speaking of freezers, if the spinach and puff have just come out of yours, you can thaw frozen puff quickly by blasting it in 15-second increments in the microwave – just enough to be able to unroll and cut. Frozen spinach can be similarly blasted in 30-second increments until you can pull it apart, then squeeze out the excess moisture before adding it to the pan.

Traditionally, you would use suluguni, a saltier mozzarella-style Georgian cheese, but I’ve made up a more globally available mix of cheeses, including cottage cheese for bonus protein.

375g packet all-butter puff pastry 2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil ½ bunch spring onions (scallions; about 200g), finely sliced 1kg bunch of greens, such as silverbeet (Swiss chard), rainbow chard or beet greens 3–4 garlic cloves , chopped 1 tbsp khmeli suneli spice mix (shop-bought or make your own, recipe below); optional but excellent 250g frozen spinach 200g mozzarella , grated 200g cottage cheese 100g feta ½ bunch dill (about 40g), stems and fronds finely chopped Zest of 1 lemon (reserve the nude lemon) 1 tsp salt flakes ¼ tsp freshly ground black pepper

Preheat your oven to 200C and line two baking trays with baking paper.

Cut the frozen puff pastry into isosceles triangles; you should get at least eight “sails”. Place on the baking trays and bake for 15 minutes, or until golden and puffed to the hilt.

Remove the pastry from the oven and rest for 15 minutes before serving.

While the pastry is puffing in the oven, heat the olive oil in a large, deep, heavy-based pan over medium heat. Add the spring onion and wait for the sizzle, then drop the heat to medium-low, pop a lid on and set a timer for five minutes.

Meanwhile, rinse your greens well (they get especially gritty towards the root end), then strip the leaves off and finely slice against the grain.Finely slice the tender parts of the stems as well.

Add the greens stems to the pan, mixing well, then reset the timer for another five minutes, stirring occasionally. Stir in the garlic and khmeli suneli, if using, and cook for another minute.

Pile in the finely chopped leafy greens and the spinach (frozen or thawed). Put the lid on and leave to wilt for three minutes. Using pan-friendly tongs, move the softened leaves from the bottom of the pan to the top, then replace the lid and cook for another three minutes. Stir again, then cook, uncovered, for another three to four minutes, until the leaves are completely wilted, thawed and well mixed through.

In a large bowl, mix together the mozzarella, cottage cheese, feta, dill and lemon zest, using a wooden spoon to break up the feta and combine. Season with the salt flakes and black pepper.

Switch the heat off under the greens and stir the cheese mix through, letting the residual heat bring it all together. Check again for seasoning.

To serve, poke the pastry sails over the top of the pan. Serve at the table on a trivet, with the reserved lemon cheeks in a small bowl alongside. Using a serving spoon, scoop the cheesy greens on to each plate, then top with a pastry sail or two.

Khmeli suneli is Georgia’s version of curry powder or garam masala – which means every household has its own twist. If you can only find whole fenugreek seeds, halve the quantity, as freshly ground is more intensely bitter. Blue fenugreek is ideal if you can find it, as this is what we’d use in Georgia. Any time you want to bring some Georgian spice to your life, grab this out of the pantry and give it a shake over steamed greens, on proteins as a rub or finishing spice, and through creamy dressings and omelettes.

2 tbsp ground coriander , 10g 2 tbsp dried basil , 5g 2 tbsp dried oregano , 5g 2 tsp ground fennel seeds , 5g 2 tbsp ground fenugreek , 20g (halve the quantity if grinding the seeds yourself) 2 tbsp ground turmeric , 20g ½ tsp cayenne pepper , 2g

Measure all your spices into a clean jar with a tight-fitting lid. (I like to use digital scales when measuring spices, which is why I’ve included all the gram weights here.) Firmly close the lid and shake the spices about until evenly mixed.

Storage and shelf life: use right away, or store in a cool, dark nook of the pantry, where your spice mix will keep for up to six months. Give the jar a good shake before using.

This is an edited extract from Weeknights with Alice by Alice Zaslavsky, photography by Rochelle Eagle, available now through Murdoch Books (AU$49.99)

articles.content:
Mason Reeves steals the show as an eight year old who stumbles across a sex assault but, despite strong performances, parts of the film feel contrived

B eth de Araújo’s new movie takes a very big swing, and it has won prizes and acclaim since its premiere at Sundance. I was unsure about some of the film’s high-concept ideas but the lead performance from its eight-year-old newcomer Mason Reeves is outstanding. Those concerned about spoilers had better look away.

Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan play Damien and Claire, a smart professional couple in San Francisco with a bright young daughter called Josephine, marvellously played by Reeves. Damien takes Josephine to Golden Gate Park one morning to play football (they turn out to enjoy watching the English Premier League on TV). She mischievously runs on ahead of her dad to a secluded spot in the park where Damien can’t immediately find her and it is there that Josephine witnesses a rape – not less horrifying for being filmed in long shot.

Damien catches up with Josephine, and gives chase to the rapist; Josephine and the rape victim find themselves in the back of a police car while the cops and Damien deal with matters, almost as if they are culprits and prisoners. Deeply affected by something she cannot understand or process in her mind, Josephine starts acting out in school, not helped by Damien bizarrely insisting she take self-defence classes. Her disorientation borders on psychosis, and all the time the court date nears when Josephine has to give evidence in front of a jury.

There are some strong moments here, but also moments when Damien and Claire’s furious rows look like an acting improv class. And the big motif of the whole film is that the rapist himself keeps appearing silently in scenes, like a ghost that only Josephine can see. Of course, this arguably approximates what many people in this situation can experience, but after a while it feels contrived. The victim herself is supposedly going to be absent from court, not being subject to a subpoena, but the procedural chill of this plot point is cancelled when she arrives at the end to give courageous Josephine an emotional thank you for her evidence.

And the verdict? It is not actually shown. The defence tries to undermine Josephine’s testimony and suggest something more complex was going on, some consensual role-play, but the film itself does not create any complexity or ambiguity arising from what Josephine saw and from what we see from her point of view. Perhaps the point is that the verdict is not relevant, as Josephine and her parents will still have to get on with their lives and deal with the after-effects of this trauma. That’s fair enough, although in the real world the verdict would surely be very important. So some misjudgments here – but Reeves is impressive.

articles.title: How sensitive data from Centrelink and other Australian agencies may have been fed to Palantir software
articles.summary: Exclusive: Personal information of Centrelink clients and childcare workers is among data shared with ACIC, which uses US tech company’s software The personal information of Centrelink customers, taxpayers and childcare workers is among a trove of sensitive data that may be ending up in Palantir’s surveillance software in Australia, without the departments responsible for the information even knowing about it. As Guardian Australia reported in September , Palantir’s software is used by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC) as part of the multi-agency fraud fusion taskforce, which was established in 2022 with the goal of targeting fraud in government payments from the national disability insurance scheme, childcare and welfare. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Exclusive: Personal information of Centrelink clients and childcare workers is among data shared with ACIC, which uses US tech company’s software

T he personal information of Centrelink customers, taxpayers and childcare workers is among a trove of sensitive data that may be ending up in Palantir’s surveillance software in Australia, without the departments responsible for the information even knowing about it.

As Guardian Australia reported in September , Palantir’s software is used by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC) as part of the multi-agency fraud fusion taskforce, which was established in 2022 with the goal of targeting fraud in government payments from the national disability insurance scheme, childcare and welfare.

New documents, released under freedom of information requests, reveal the extent to which at least 10 government agencies share sensitive data with the taskforce, which could be fed into Palantir’s software.

The controversial US tech company, co-founded by the Donald Trump-aligned billionaire Peter Thiel , has clients including the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that use the software to analyse vast amounts of data.

While the company has insisted it has no access to the data clients enter into the software, the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has led calls for a ban on Palantir contracts with the Australian government.

In April, the company implied some cultures were inferior to others in a 22-point manifesto posted on X and described by one UK MP as the “ramblings of a supervillain”. Shoebridge has said Palantir should not be near Australian data given how the data mining software is used by the IDF and ICE.

The Australian government has spent nearly $80m on Palantir contracts since May .

The taskforce is headed up by the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) and Services Australia. The intelligence program – known as the fraud fusion centre – is led by the ACIC, and brings in “large volumes of information, data and intelligence” held by agencies that could be relevant to the taskforce work, according to the documents released under FoI.

The FoI requests, undertaken by Dr Gabrielle Josling, an independent researcher and data scientist, showed at least 10 federal agencies were sharing data with the ACIC – data that could ultimately be put in Palantir’s software by the commission.

Documents from the Department of Education show the ACIC is “collecting criminal intelligence and analysing and crossmatching data” from sources including:

The personal information authorised by Services Australia to be obtained by the ACIC includes names, date of birth, information about proof of ID, addresses, telephone numbers, Centrelink claims or reviews, itemised income and asset details, employer information, bank account information and “surveillance material” held by the agency.

The collected data is held by the fraud fusion centre and, while a privacy impact assessment noted that the ACIC is not subject to the Privacy Act, the agency’s protocols state it acts in accordance with the Australian privacy principles “wherever reasonably consistent with the effective performance of its statutory functions”.

Services Australia said each disclosure to the ACIC was considered on a case-by-case basis. There had been two disclosures in the financial year to date, compared with 21 in 2025-26 and 47 in 2024-25.

The ATO’s documents do not reveal the extent of the data provided by the agency but state that tax file numbers cannot be provided under law. It made 758 disclosures between November 2022 and July 2026, including 376 to the NDIA and 42 to the ACIC.

A spokesperson for the ATO told Guardian Australia the taxpayer information was disclosed where it was “lawfully able” to do so under the terms of the memorandum of understanding as part of the taskforce, the ATO’s intelligence disclosure governance plan and the Tax Administration Act.

The federal education department has withheld releasing information about what data it has provided to the taskforce but the documents state it is data related to the childcare subsidy scheme.

A spokesperson for the department refused to comment on “detailed operational information-sharing arrangements” and directed questions about Palantir use to the ACIC.

The ACIC said data handling is subject to agreements with the agency supplying the data, and that Palantir was “part of a suite of analytical tools to undertake analysis on specific cases to assist partner agencies to disrupt serious organised crime networks defrauding government programs”.

The agency did not respond to questions from Guardian Australia on whether other federal agencies were informed if the data provided was ingested into Palantir’s software. Neither the ATO nor Centrelink were aware if Palantir was used.

“The use of software by another agency is a question for that agency, and any questions relating to ACIC use of data obtained under the FFT are best directed to the ACIC,” an ATO spokesperson said.

The documents reveal that the memorandum of understanding in 2024 between taskforce agencies originally required the taskforce to develop an ethics and human oversight framework governing the control of the information shared. It was described as “an important part of effective risk management for the FFT”.

But correspondence released from September 2025 reveals that it was determined that the process was “too difficult to implement” and the framework instead became an “ethics guide” in October last year.

In a submission to the Australian National Audit Office’s review into the taskforce, Josling said the new model abandoned requirements for defined assessments and reviews of the taskforce. A framework for evaluating and monitoring the performance of the taskforce was also not developed.

“A multi-agency taskforce needs a way to learn from data quality problems, data matching limitations, unproductive referrals, emerging risks, and weaknesses in governance,” Josling said in the submission.

Companies and governments have faced pressure to stop using Palantir, with both Coles and Westpac reportedly deciding against renewing their contracts with the firm. The UK government has also faced pressure to drop its contracts with Palantir , including a contract with the NHS.

Palantir has maintained that it does not have access to the data clients enter into its software. A spokesperson has previously defended the company’s contracts with the Australian government, saying it is just a software company.

“We are committed to supporting Australian government agencies in tackling complex challenges, including serious financial crime and fraud,” they said.

articles.title: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
articles.summary: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry. Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true

T he resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry.

Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet.

The scandal has thrown Nvidia into crisis, cast a pall over the AI boom and even threatened the stability of the US economy. Huang’s downfall is a nightmare scenario for a tech industry that has become increasingly fearful of security threats, and a glimpse into what intelligence experts say is a constant theater of corporate espionage secretly playing out every day throughout the US.

“The reason that this is making the news is because obviously you have one of the wealthiest men in the world and one of the highest-profile CEOs in the world,” said Don Aviv, the CEO of corporate intelligence firm Interfor International. “But this happens all the time, across industries.”

As the AI boom and geopolitical competition with China have ramped up in recent years, the tech industry and security officials have tried to prevent exactly the type of plot that allegedly ensnared Huang. Corporate intelligence firms, AI companies and US officials have been on alert for espionage operations targeting tech executives – with some major tech firms warning employees to be skeptical of their personal relationships and holding investigations into how executives could be compromised.

OpenAI has even held training sessions specifically running through “honeypot” scenarios where a corporate spy or foreign intelligence asset pursues a sexual relationship with company staff in return for information or leverage, according to the Wall Street Journal . Aviv meanwhile estimated that his firm alone has conducted around a dozen investigations for significant companies into schemes involving honeypots, personal relationships, coercion or blackmail over the past three years.

Beyond a disastrous lapse in judgment from Huang, experts also describe the affair with a suspected spy as a massive failure of corporate oversight and a remarkable triumph for an alleged foreign influence operation. For all the concerns about digital infrastructure and the growth of cyber-attacks, intelligence analysts say that human error remains the most vulnerable part of most companies.

“The honeypot style trap is as old as the earth itself,” said Randy Watt, head of the corporate threat assessment and consulting firm SRW. “It speaks to a consistent weakness in humans that is exploitable.

“I guarantee you there are a whole number of executives in powerful corporations that are reviewing their relationships with girlfriends,” Watt added.

OpenAI, Meta and Google did not return requests for comment on their security practices. Nvidia did not comment on questions about Huang’s affairs or when the company learned about his involvement with the alleged spy. The Chinese government has denied any involvement in the affair or efforts at corporate espionage, with a Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson earlier this week calling the reports “nothing but a smear against China”.

The fallout from allegations that China conducted a high-profile foreign intelligence operation against Huang has had global implications on the market and tech industry, with the Nasdaq falling 4% immediately after Huang’s resignation and Nvidia losing hundreds of billions in market value this week. Yet security experts say that while the impact of the operation is unique, the tactics and goals are not.

Silicon Valley, flush with incredibly valuable intellectual property and trade secrets, has long been a prized target for foreign spying operations. Throughout the cold war, Soviet agents conducted a decades-long effort to steal technological secrets from US tech firms, including major chip companies, that involved a complex web of international espionage.

During the 1970s and 80s, Soviet intelligence officers operated out of the Russian consulate in San Francisco as they carried out spying operations, according to former FBI special agent Rick Smith, who spent over two decades in the Bay Area working in counterintelligence. US officials estimated at the time that the Moscow Kremlin had mobilized thousands of spies in the country with the intent to steal intellectual property and help the Soviet Union copy American technology they could not produce themselves.

“Gaining access to our advanced technology continues to be their top priority,” William Casey, director of the CIA, warned in 1985.

Other countries and foreign nationals have also launched their own corporate espionage operations. North Korean spies created two businesses in the US with the intent of spreading malicious software to infect cryptocurrency developers, Reuters and cybersecurity firms reported last year. In October, US authorities arrested a Saudi national accused of planting a sophisticated listening device within the headquarters of OpenAI.

In recent years, however, it’s China’s government that has been most prominently accused of a multilayered effort to steal technological capabilities and IP from US tech firms.

A report from the nonprofit Center for Strategic and International Studies found at least 224 incidents of Chinese espionage in the US between 2000 and 2022, with over half of the plots directed at the theft of commercial technologies. In January, a federal jury in California convicted a former Google engineer of stealing confidential company information to benefit the Chinese government.

Some operations linked to China have even involved honeypot-style schemes where a suspected spy has pursued personal or sexual relationships with politicians and executives. The Washington Post obtained declassified FBI documents in August that showed that former California congressman Eric Swalwell admitted to “occasionally hooking up” with suspected Chinese operative Christine Fang.

The alleged Chinese operation involving Huang stood out to security experts, however, for both the extremely high-profile target and its apparent success.

Huang was first seen with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive who ran the Singapore-based Megaspeed datacenter firm, in late 2023. The two were together at a bar in Taiwan in 2024 and again at a conference in 2025, by which time the US commerce department was investigating whether Megaspeed was diverting AI chips to China in violation of export controls. In spring of this year, state secretary Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo reporting that the Nvidia CEO was in a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy based on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times . Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang ultimately appears to have helped facilitate the transfer of billions of dollars in advanced Nvidia chips to China.

“As an American, it’s not good, but I’m impressed with their skills,” Smith, the former FBI counterintelligence official, said. “What a target and a tremendous job by the Chinese.”

Huang was not only the head of what was once the world’s most valuable company, but he is also a close ally of Donald Trump who accompanied the president at White House dinners and on Trump’s official state visit to China. Huang has been an influential voice on tech policy, especially on export control and open source AI model issues, although it is unclear whether his extramarital relationship had any bearing on his views. Trump backed Huang after the scandal, calling him an “honorable guy”.

The Trump administration is also facing questions over why Alice Huang’s firm Megaspeed was spared from being placed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, Axios reported , despite intelligence outlining issues with the company. US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick is under pressure to resign over perceived inaction in response to problems with Megaspeed.

Nvidia has since announced that it hired a top US law firm to conduct an investigation into Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, while Trump stated that the FBI would launch its own probe into the affair. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress and he now faces a lawsuit in California accusing him of misleading shareholders.

In order to combat the wave of corporate espionage and foreign influence campaigns, many companies have turned to intelligence and threat assessment firms to harden their security – several of which say they are expecting more demand for their services after the Nvidia scandal. These firms hold training and conduct investigations into what makes a company vulnerable, often focusing on the human elements of security.

“Everybody thinks it’s like what we see in Hollywood – surreptitious entry and listening devices and bugs and tails,” said Eduardo Jany, head of global security for a major US corporation. “It’s really more about social engineering.”

Malicious actors will seek out staff at companies that hold positions of influence or valuable information, frequently using what is publicly available through social media and data brokers to learn their personal information and create targeted plans. An employee with a substance abuse or gambling problem provides one avenue of exploitation, experts said, while a staffer who is lonely and seeking out relationships offers another kind of vulnerability.

Attempts at corporate espionage can also often come in the guise of business opportunities, as it appears was potentially the case with Nvidia and Huang, with spies posing as fellow tech executives or financiers.

“They’re looking at easy access and proximity from conferences and customer relationships,” Jany said. “They sidle up to our executives at any events or trade shows, or even make promises of investments.”

Corporations will sometimes hire firms to conduct what’s called penetration testing to check for weak points in their security, which involves using simulated attacks to uncover real vulnerabilities. One security expert described an example of his firm following an employee to the parking lot of a grocery store in order to gain access to their car and take a corporate ID card left hanging from their rearview mirror.

Dealing with C-suite executives like Huang tends to pose its own unique challenges for security and threat assessment firms, experts said. Top leadership at companies possesses far more autonomy and authority than the average employee, making it harder for underlings to confront them about misconduct or potential risks. CEOs can also be hostile to seeing themselves as fallible, with consultants having to sensitively approach the idea that their personal relationships may not be what they seem.

Executives can also protest that they’re not important enough to be a target or that everything about them is already public.

“It’s a defense mechanism to being told that the way you live your life is going to have to change,” said Elizabeth Buckley, Teneo’s head of cyber and technical solutions.

One question facing Nvidia is who within the company knew about Huang’s relationships and whether any concerns were raised internally. paragraphs: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true

T he resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry.

Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet.

The scandal has thrown Nvidia into crisis, cast a pall over the AI boom and even threatened the stability of the US economy. Huang’s downfall is a nightmare scenario for a tech industry that has become increasingly fearful of security threats, and a glimpse into what intelligence experts say is a constant theater of corporate espionage secretly playing out every day throughout the US.

“The reason that this is making the news is because obviously you have one of the wealthiest men in the world and one of the highest-profile CEOs in the world,” said Don Aviv, the CEO of corporate intelligence firm Interfor International. “But this happens all the time, across industries.”

As the AI boom and geopolitical competition with China have ramped up in recent years, the tech industry and security officials have tried to prevent exactly the type of plot that allegedly ensnared Huang. Corporate intelligence firms, AI companies and US officials have been on alert for espionage operations targeting tech executives – with some major tech firms warning employees to be skeptical of their personal relationships and holding investigations into how executives could be compromised.

OpenAI has even held training sessions specifically running through “honeypot” scenarios where a corporate spy or foreign intelligence asset pursues a sexual relationship with company staff in return for information or leverage, according to the Wall Street Journal . Aviv meanwhile estimated that his firm alone has conducted around a dozen investigations for significant companies into schemes involving honeypots, personal relationships, coercion or blackmail over the past three years.

Beyond a disastrous lapse in judgment from Huang, experts also describe the affair with a suspected spy as a massive failure of corporate oversight and a remarkable triumph for an alleged foreign influence operation. For all the concerns about digital infrastructure and the growth of cyber-attacks, intelligence analysts say that human error remains the most vulnerable part of most companies.

“The honeypot style trap is as old as the earth itself,” said Randy Watt, head of the corporate threat assessment and consulting firm SRW. “It speaks to a consistent weakness in humans that is exploitable.
“I guarantee you there are a whole number of executives in powerful corporations that are reviewing their relationships with girlfriends,” Watt added.

OpenAI, Meta and Google did not return requests for comment on their security practices. Nvidia did not comment on questions about Huang’s affairs or when the company learned about his involvement with the alleged spy. The Chinese government has denied any involvement in the affair or efforts at corporate espionage, with a Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson earlier this week calling the reports “nothing but a smear against China”.

The fallout from allegations that China conducted a high-profile foreign intelligence operation against Huang has had global implications on the market and tech industry, with the Nasdaq falling 4% immediately after Huang’s resignation and Nvidia losing hundreds of billions in market value this week. Yet security experts say that while the impact of the operation is unique, the tactics and goals are not.

Silicon Valley, flush with incredibly valuable intellectual property and trade secrets, has long been a prized target for foreign spying operations. Throughout the cold war, Soviet agents conducted a decades-long effort to steal technological secrets from US tech firms, including major chip companies, that involved a complex web of international espionage.

During the 1970s and 80s, Soviet intelligence officers operated out of the Russian consulate in San Francisco as they carried out spying operations, according to former FBI special agent Rick Smith, who spent over two decades in the Bay Area working in counterintelligence. US officials estimated at the time that the Moscow Kremlin had mobilized thousands of spies in the country with the intent to steal intellectual property and help the Soviet Union copy American technology they could not produce themselves.
“Gaining access to our advanced technology continues to be their top priority,” William Casey, director of the CIA, warned in 1985.

Other countries and foreign nationals have also launched their own corporate espionage operations. North Korean spies created two businesses in the US with the intent of spreading malicious software to infect cryptocurrency developers, Reuters and cybersecurity firms reported last year. In October, US authorities arrested a Saudi national accused of planting a sophisticated listening device within the headquarters of OpenAI.
In recent years, however, it’s China’s government that has been most prominently accused of a multilayered effort to steal technological capabilities and IP from US tech firms.

A report from the nonprofit Center for Strategic and International Studies found at least 224 incidents of Chinese espionage in the US between 2000 and 2022, with over half of the plots directed at the theft of commercial technologies. In January, a federal jury in California convicted a former Google engineer of stealing confidential company information to benefit the Chinese government.

Some operations linked to China have even involved honeypot-style schemes where a suspected spy has pursued personal or sexual relationships with politicians and executives. The Washington Post obtained declassified FBI documents in August that showed that former California congressman Eric Swalwell admitted to “occasionally hooking up” with suspected Chinese operative Christine Fang.
The alleged Chinese operation involving Huang stood out to security experts, however, for both the extremely high-profile target and its apparent success.

Huang was first seen with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive who ran the Singapore-based Megaspeed datacenter firm, in late 2023. The two were together at a bar in Taiwan in 2024 and again at a conference in 2025, by which time the US commerce department was investigating whether Megaspeed was diverting AI chips to China in violation of export controls. In spring of this year, state secretary Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo reporting that the Nvidia CEO was in a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy based on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times . Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang ultimately appears to have helped facilitate the transfer of billions of dollars in advanced Nvidia chips to China.
“As an American, it’s not good, but I’m impressed with their skills,” Smith, the former FBI counterintelligence official, said. “What a target and a tremendous job by the Chinese.”

Huang was not only the head of what was once the world’s most valuable company, but he is also a close ally of Donald Trump who accompanied the president at White House dinners and on Trump’s official state visit to China. Huang has been an influential voice on tech policy, especially on export control and open source AI model issues, although it is unclear whether his extramarital relationship had any bearing on his views. Trump backed Huang after the scandal, calling him an “honorable guy”.

The Trump administration is also facing questions over why Alice Huang’s firm Megaspeed was spared from being placed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, Axios reported , despite intelligence outlining issues with the company. US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick is under pressure to resign over perceived inaction in response to problems with Megaspeed.

Nvidia has since announced that it hired a top US law firm to conduct an investigation into Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, while Trump stated that the FBI would launch its own probe into the affair. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress and he now faces a lawsuit in California accusing him of misleading shareholders.

In order to combat the wave of corporate espionage and foreign influence campaigns, many companies have turned to intelligence and threat assessment firms to harden their security – several of which say they are expecting more demand for their services after the Nvidia scandal. These firms hold training and conduct investigations into what makes a company vulnerable, often focusing on the human elements of security.

“Everybody thinks it’s like what we see in Hollywood – surreptitious entry and listening devices and bugs and tails,” said Eduardo Jany, head of global security for a major US corporation. “It’s really more about social engineering.”

Malicious actors will seek out staff at companies that hold positions of influence or valuable information, frequently using what is publicly available through social media and data brokers to learn their personal information and create targeted plans. An employee with a substance abuse or gambling problem provides one avenue of exploitation, experts said, while a staffer who is lonely and seeking out relationships offers another kind of vulnerability.

Attempts at corporate espionage can also often come in the guise of business opportunities, as it appears was potentially the case with Nvidia and Huang, with spies posing as fellow tech executives or financiers.

“They’re looking at easy access and proximity from conferences and customer relationships,” Jany said. “They sidle up to our executives at any events or trade shows, or even make promises of investments.”

Corporations will sometimes hire firms to conduct what’s called penetration testing to check for weak points in their security, which involves using simulated attacks to uncover real vulnerabilities. One security expert described an example of his firm following an employee to the parking lot of a grocery store in order to gain access to their car and take a corporate ID card left hanging from their rearview mirror.

articles.title: World Cup 2026: England frustrated; Scotland face Brazil; Infantino defends hydration breaks – live

Continue reading...
articles.content:
At the start of the competition, it didn’t look like a 1-0 win and two one-goal defeats would be enough for Scotland, but now, that seems likely to qualify them. However, Brazil looked much better in their second game than their first – admittedly against far worse opposition, but it did also look like Carlo Ancelotti is clover to finding his best team. Against Morocco, I was shocked to see Igor Thiago selected ahead of Matheus Cunha; I think we can safely say that will not happen again.

Which I guess brings us to our next round of action. Before we properly dig in, let’s acquaint ourselves with the panoply of permutations.

Colombia played pretty well, I thought, and would’ve won by more were it not for Lionel Mpasi in the DRC net. I was disappointed by the winner because on first look, I thought Daniel Muñoz had done him with the eyes, but it turned out to be a deflection.

Panama have come on loads since England clattered them in 2018 – Ghana also got away with it against them. Luka Modric, though, what a player.

Qatar’s manager, Julen Lopetegui, has revealed Assim Madibo spent the eve of their final Group A match visiting Ismael Kone after the Canada midfielder underwent successful surgery for a broken leg.

Madibo was sent off after inadvertently injuring Kone in last week’s 6-0 defeat to Canada. At the time Madibo was visibly distraught and he has since visited Kone in Vancouver, Canada’s base for the tournament. Kone, who plays in Serie A for Sassuolo, is expected to miss at least five months of action. “It has been very tough for him,” Lopetegui said of Madibo on Tuesday afternoon. “We wish him [Kone] all the best to recover as soon as possible. “Now in the current moment Madibo is in Vancouver visiting Kone because he was very, very affected by this injury – it was never his intention. It was a very clear accident. We wish him all the best.” Madibo is suspended for Qatar’s match against Bosnia and Herzegovina in Seattle on Wednesday. Homam Ahmed is also suspended after being sent off in the same game last Thursday.

Iran prepared for their final Group G match by highlighting the US’s deadly attack on a school that killed at least 168 people, predominantly schoolchildren. Iran’s players trained at their base in Tijuana, Mexico, on Tuesday evening with black corner flags adorned with the message: “#168” . The number refers to the victims who were killed in a strike on an elementary school in Minab, southern Iran, on 28 February, the first day of the US-Israel war on Iran. The attack was attributed to the US military, with Donald Trump last week saying: “Nobody did that on purpose. Mistakes are made. The war is nasty.” When Iran first landed at their base in Mexico earlier this month, after a training camp in Turkey, they arrived wearing pin badges on their lapels that read: “#168”. Iran will arrive in Seattle from Tijuana at 11.30am local time on Wednesday before facing Egypt on Friday after being granted special permission to arrive in the US two days before the game. The match is the World Cup’s designated Pride Match, despite both teams complaining to Fifa about the celebrations which will coincide with Seattle’s Pride weekend. After Sunday’s draw with Belgium, Iran left a handwritten note in the dressing room at Los Angeles Stadium in which they called for peace. The message, which also featured #168, read: ““From the ancient Persia of thousands of years ago to the civilised Iran of today, the spirit of Iran remains alive and steadfast. We came to Los Angeles with pride, competed with honour, and leave with dignity “Thank you Los Angeles for your hospitality. And thank you to every Iranian who gave their heart, voice and soul for Iran throughout these 180 minutes. May peace, respect and friendship prevail among all nations.”

Fifa’s view of Iran training with #168 flags remains to be seen. Their regulations state that “equipment must not have any political, religious or personal slogans, statements or images” or players and/or the team may be sanctioned by the competition organiser.

Iran were only permitted to arrive in LA before draws against New Zealand and Belgium 24 hours before the games, leading their head coach, Amir Ghalenoei to label Iran the “most oppressed” team at the tournament.

Also at training on Tuesday, the former Brighton winger Alireza Jahanbakshsh was given a commemorative Iran shirt after reaching 100 caps for his country against Belgium. Fifa has been contacted for comment.

I don’t want to get all conspiracist, but you don’t have be John Le Carré to wonder if TV companies benefitting from ad revenue has an upside for Fifa even though they’re not cut in on each specific deal.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino has defended the introduction of hydration breaks at the World Cup , insisting that for football’s ⁠governing body they are driven purely by sporting considerations and not commercial interests.

This has fuelled debate over their impact on the game, with some viewers complaining about ⁠being exposed to commercials during the three-minute stoppages.

“There is no additional revenue for Fifa, as all ​commercial agreements were signed well in advance. ‌So, this is not ‌a financial issue for us. For us, it is purely a sporting matter,” Infantino said in ‌a statement on Wednesday.

The breaks allow coaching staff to give in-game tactical instructions, a shift critics say disrupts match momentum and fundamentally alters the nature of the game.

England manager Thomas Tuchel said the additional break “interrupts and changes the identity of the football match“, while Uruguay coach Marcelo Bielsa said dividing matches into shorter segments takes away the fundamental characteristic ‌of the game.

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente and Netherlands captain Virgil van Dijk have supported the intent behind the rule in extreme heat, but questioned ​the need for it in cooler conditions and at covered venues.

“The main reason is the heat, but we also have to understand that in a competition like the (FIFA) World Cup, played over 39 days, with teams potentially playing eight matches in those 39 days, having a moment to rest ⁠is extremely important,” Infantino said.

“What matters even more to us is ensuring ​that all teams, in every ​match, are playing under the ​same conditions.

“It’s very difficult to accept that a coach might have the opportunity ​to influence a ‌match by making adjustments ​simply because it’s ​hotter, while in another match, where the temperature is slightly lower, the same coach doesn’t have the same opportunity.”

Infantino added that the breaks had not reduced the intensity of matches, suggesting players were able to maintain a high level of performance throughout games.

“Is it possible we all got over excited by England beating an old and possibly quite poor Croatia team (who laboured to a 1-0 win over Panama)?” wonders Samuel Dodson. “Tuchel’s record against any reasonable side seems to be losses against Japan and Senegal and a draw against another ailing once-decent side in Uruguay. Friendlies don’t really matter, of course; and that second half surge for 15 minutes really was very fun. And not very much like how we expect England to play. This stodgy draw against Ghana however is exactly how I expect England to play. Remember 0-0 against Algeria? The USA? The good news of course is that the performance and result means we can go back to what we do best – endless debate and faux controversy and anger over team selections. Had we beaten Ghana comfortably here in not sure we or the media would have quite known how to react or what to talk about.”

Croatia definitely played into England’s hands, but the way they took control of the game was impressive. Watching it, my sense was that at some point, the defence would let them down, and Japan are a particularly difficult opponent for how they’re trying to play – so too Spain – but on a good day they can beat anyone and even on a bad day, they’ve the attacking talent to save themselves. Do I think they’re likely champions? No, but I don’t think it’s impossible.

Remember 2018, when Emmanuel Macron got drenched as Vladimir Putin relaxed under an umbrella held for him? How will Trump assert himself to this level?

I was really disappointed with Reece James. He’s a superb player capable of so much better going forward and England really needed that from him – overlaps, underlaps and crosses. But he delivered almost nothing.

Email! “‘I don’t care about Messi’ was such an insulting and insensitive remark from such a talented player,” says Krishnamoorthy V of Ronaldo. “This is what ego does to your personality. Ghana sending CR7 and co home will be so satisfying.”

I think that imperviousness has made Ronaldo what he is. Of course, he’s not really impervious at all, but thinks he is, and that’s all that matters.

Jacob makes a fair point here, that Palmer and Foden didn’t do enough to force their way into the squad. But both are special talents who’ve shown quality miles beyond that which we’ve seen from Madueke and Gordon, who are not, and neither of whom were all that good last season either.

Again, though, I come back to the big-space/small-space thing, and the lack of balance in the squad. And, judging by the substitutions, it’s not something management see as an issue – the changes were like for like, rather than seeking to alter or vary the method of attack.

The good news for England is that, as they progress, teams will, most likely, look to attack them, leaving space for their speed and physicality to exploit. But the squad lack guile and magic, completely unnecessarily, and it’s not clear Tuchel really groks that.

Anderson, Rice and Bellingham are all fantastic players, but none have the deftness around the box to play quick combinations, or the eye to thread through little passes. It was obvious at half-time that, given what was available, the wise move was to hook one of the first two for Kobbie Mainoo, who is brilliant at finding space in traffic.

Or, in other words, a balanced midfield is not three power-players; at least one touch-player is required, and Mainoo is the only one England have. Perhaps you might say Eberechi Eze is that too, and he came on far too late to influence the game or for it to look like the coaching staff are on top of the problem.

I agree with Barney here: this was a small-space game, in which England used big-space players.

Partly this is because of the squad Thomas Tuchel picked. If I was facing England and you offered me Noni Madueke, Cole Palmer and Phil Foden, I know which of those three I’d back myself against. Madueke is a decent player, but no more than that; he isn’t special, and the other two are.

Palmer, in particular, has the ability to change the pace of a game and do surprising things others can’t, exactly what you need against an organised low block. But that wast the only glaring issue: Lewis Hall would’ve given England natural width on the left and also excellent passing out of defence, but he’s not even in the squad; and, though Trent Alexander-Arnold is no one’s idea of a proper defender, if you’re using him it’s because you need a goal, and leaving his delivery and craft at home makes absolutely no sense.

I wonder if these errors reflect a manager unfamiliar with tournament football; Tuchel has decided to play a particular way, and picked a collection of profiles he thinks can do that. But that’s left him without the means to change things properly; if things go wrong, he can swap players, but what if, as yesterday, the issue is the system and its principles?

And was Jordan Pickford fortunate not to get a red card when he hared out of box to collide with Abdul Fatawu?

I feel not. Had Fatawu got a touch on the ball, Pickford was toast, but because neither player did, I don’t think we can say there was a foul. Both went for it, both missed, so it makes most sense is to call it a collision.

I don’t really see how you can’t give it. Fatawu was in and Konsa launches into him, getting nowhere near the ball with no chance of getting at the ball – which makes it a red card too.

As far as goalless draws go, I thought it an engaging one. But plenty of things for Thomas Tuchel to ponder, which we’ll dig into into which we’ll dig presently.

This “I’m back” situation, though; it’ll take more than bagging a brace against Uzbekistan for that to be so.

Roberto Martínez has options, too. He could play a wide player up front – Pedro Neto has done it for Chelsea – or Goncalo Ramos, who’s a striker.

But it’s not just Ronaldo preventing this team from working as it should – Bernardo Silva was left out and, if they’re to fulfil their potential – they’ve got the players to win the thing – he must surely play a key role. I’d get him into a midfield three with Vitinha and João Neves, then have Bruno Fernandes and Neto with free roles behind – if we must – Ronaldo.

Surely no one rhose surname isn’t Dos Santos Aveiro really thinks that, though? Ronaldo can still finish – he’ll never lose that – but it’s very hard to even come up with rationale, never mind believe rationale, that says the best version of this Portugal team contains him.

We go again! We’ll begin by reflecting on the latest action – Portugal getting their competition going by thrashing Uzbekistan, England and Ghana near-enough securing passage to the knockouts, Croatia just about seeing off Panama, now eliminated, and Colombia forcing their way past DR Congo.

Then, when we’ve done that, we’ll build up to today’s action, featuring the final round of matches in Group B – Switzerland v Canada and Bosnia and Herzegovina v Qatar; Group C – Morocco v Haiti and Scotland v Brazil… and Group A – South Africa v South Korea and Czechia v México.

I reckon some people might have some thoughts about all of that lot, so we’ll share those of our writers, but do send in yours too.

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente and Netherlands captain Virgil van Dijk have supported the intent behind the rule in extreme heat, but questioned ​the need for it in cooler conditions and at covered venues.

“The main reason is the heat, but we also have to understand that in a competition like the (FIFA) World Cup, played over 39 days, with teams potentially playing eight matches in those 39 days, having a moment to rest ⁠is extremely important,” Infantino said.
“What matters even more to us is ensuring ​that all teams, in every ​match, are playing under the ​same conditions.

“It’s very difficult to accept that a coach might have the opportunity ​to influence a ‌match by making adjustments ​simply because it’s ​hotter, while in another match, where the temperature is slightly lower, the same coach doesn’t have the same opportunity.”
Infantino added that the breaks had not reduced the intensity of matches, suggesting players were able to maintain a high level of performance throughout games.

“Is it possible we all got over excited by England beating an old and possibly quite poor Croatia team (who laboured to a 1-0 win over Panama)?” wonders Samuel Dodson. “Tuchel’s record against any reasonable side seems to be losses against Japan and Senegal and a draw against another ailing once-decent side in Uruguay. Friendlies don’t really matter, of course; and that second half surge for 15 minutes really was very fun. And not very much like how we expect England to play. This stodgy draw against Ghana however is exactly how I expect England to play. Remember 0-0 against Algeria? The USA? The good news of course is that the performance and result means we can go back to what we do best – endless debate and faux controversy and anger over team selections. Had we beaten Ghana comfortably here in not sure we or the media would have quite known how to react or what to talk about.”

Croatia definitely played into England’s hands, but the way they took control of the game was impressive. Watching it, my sense was that at some point, the defence would let them down, and Japan are a particularly difficult opponent for how they’re trying to play – so too Spain – but on a good day they can beat anyone and even on a bad day, they’ve the attacking talent to save themselves. Do I think they’re likely champions? No, but I don’t think it’s impossible.
Remember 2018, when Emmanuel Macron got drenched as Vladimir Putin relaxed under an umbrella held for him? How will Trump assert himself to this level?

I was really disappointed with Reece James. He’s a superb player capable of so much better going forward and England really needed that from him – overlaps, underlaps and crosses. But he delivered almost nothing.

Email! “‘I don’t care about Messi’ was such an insulting and insensitive remark from such a talented player,” says Krishnamoorthy V of Ronaldo. “This is what ego does to your personality. Ghana sending CR7 and co home will be so satisfying.”
I think that imperviousness has made Ronaldo what he is. Of course, he’s not really impervious at all, but thinks he is, and that’s all that matters.

Jacob makes a fair point here, that Palmer and Foden didn’t do enough to force their way into the squad. But both are special talents who’ve shown quality miles beyond that which we’ve seen from Madueke and Gordon, who are not, and neither of whom were all that good last season either.

Again, though, I come back to the big-space/small-space thing, and the lack of balance in the squad. And, judging by the substitutions, it’s not something management see as an issue – the changes were like for like, rather than seeking to alter or vary the method of attack.

The good news for England is that, as they progress, teams will, most likely, look to attack them, leaving space for their speed and physicality to exploit. But the squad lack guile and magic, completely unnecessarily, and it’s not clear Tuchel really groks that.

Anderson, Rice and Bellingham are all fantastic players, but none have the deftness around the box to play quick combinations, or the eye to thread through little passes. It was obvious at half-time that, given what was available, the wise move was to hook one of the first two for Kobbie Mainoo, who is brilliant at finding space in traffic.

Or, in other words, a balanced midfield is not three power-players; at least one touch-player is required, and Mainoo is the only one England have. Perhaps you might say Eberechi Eze is that too, and he came on far too late to influence the game or for it to look like the coaching staff are on top of the problem.
I agree with Barney here: this was a small-space game, in which England used big-space players.

Partly this is because of the squad Thomas Tuchel picked. If I was facing England and you offered me Noni Madueke, Cole Palmer and Phil Foden, I know which of those three I’d back myself against. Madueke is a decent player, but no more than that; he isn’t special, and the other two are.

Palmer, in particular, has the ability to change the pace of a game and do surprising things others can’t, exactly what you need against an organised low block. But that wast the only glaring issue: Lewis Hall would’ve given England natural width on the left and also excellent passing out of defence, but he’s not even in the squad; and, though Trent Alexander-Arnold is no one’s idea of a proper defender, if you’re using him it’s because you need a goal, and leaving his delivery and craft at home makes absolutely no sense.

I wonder if these errors reflect a manager unfamiliar with tournament football; Tuchel has decided to play a particular way, and picked a collection of profiles he thinks can do that. But that’s left him without the means to change things properly; if things go wrong, he can swap players, but what if, as yesterday, the issue is the system and its principles?
And was Jordan Pickford fortunate not to get a red card when he hared out of box to collide with Abdul Fatawu?

I feel not. Had Fatawu got a touch on the ball, Pickford was toast, but because neither player did, I don’t think we can say there was a foul. Both went for it, both missed, so it makes most sense is to call it a collision.
I don’t really see how you can’t give it. Fatawu was in and Konsa launches into him, getting nowhere near the ball with no chance of getting at the ball – which makes it a red card too.
As far as goalless draws go, I thought it an engaging one. But plenty of things for Thomas Tuchel to ponder, which we’ll dig into into which we’ll dig presently.
This “I’m back” situation, though; it’ll take more than bagging a brace against Uzbekistan for that to be so.
Roberto Martínez has options, too. He could play a wide player up front – Pedro Neto has done it for Chelsea – or Goncalo Ramos, who’s a striker.

But it’s not just Ronaldo preventing this team from working as it should – Bernardo Silva was left out and, if they’re to fulfil their potential – they’ve got the players to win the thing – he must surely play a key role. I’d get him into a midfield three with Vitinha and João Neves, then have Bruno Fernandes and Neto with free roles behind – if we must – Ronaldo.

Surely no one rhose surname isn’t Dos Santos Aveiro really thinks that, though? Ronaldo can still finish – he’ll never lose that – but it’s very hard to even come up with rationale, never mind believe rationale, that says the best version of this Portugal team contains him.

We go again! We’ll begin by reflecting on the latest action – Portugal getting their competition going by thrashing Uzbekistan, England and Ghana near-enough securing passage to the knockouts, Croatia just about seeing off Panama, now eliminated, and Colombia forcing their way past DR Congo.

Then, when we’ve done that, we’ll build up to today’s action, featuring the final round of matches in Group B – Switzerland v Canada and Bosnia and Herzegovina v Qatar; Group C – Morocco v Haiti and Scotland v Brazil… and Group A – South Africa v South Korea and Czechia v México.
I reckon some people might have some thoughts about all of that lot, so we’ll share those of our writers, but do send in yours too.

articles.content:
Alex Freeman has impressed from right-back while Eli Just is catching the eye with his body swerves and goal threat

It is not difficult to see why this old head on young shoulders is destined for a big career. In a Morocco team conditioned to play first-time passes, he sets the tone with his instant decisions. Bouaddi is in essence the deepest of the midfield three and he not only plays quickly but often finds a colleague in a more forward position. Strong on the ball, he can intercept from his central position and looks to continue his involvement after playing a pass. Bouaddi can tackle and shield a ball and finds space naturally. With his height, at 6ft 1in, technique and football intelligence, he will not be a Lille player for much longer. When Bouaddi gets forward he should try to be more positive – to be a more complete player he will need to have a few goals on his CV – but he is a real talent.

Mauricio Pochettino has made a dream World Cup start with the USA. All his players have performed with pace and positivity, limiting opponents to few opportunities, and Freeman, the youngest in his squad, has caught my eye with his contributions from right-back. When a poor Australia side threatened, he made a superb last-ditch challenge, intercepting a low cross. Previously I had noticed a player cool in possession who keeps the play moving with an early pass rather a big kick upfield. Freeman left Orlando for the Spanish overachievers Villarreal in January and shows maturity beyond his years. He is also brave and, not long after a heavy clash of heads, he leaped to score the USA’s second goal against Australia . At close quarters when confronted he showed a sharp change of feet to escape an attacker and he can tackle too and has enough pace.

Playing as the left centre-back in a four-man defence, he has impressed alongside three more experienced defenders. The 6ft 4in player is in line to play a second season in Serie A with Sassuolo after the tournament, having been a major contributor to their 2025 promotion while on loan from Juventus. I would compare him to Luka Vuskovic, the Croatian who joined Tottenham last summer and went on loan to Hamburg. Muharemovic is not as aggressive in the air but wins his share of headers and I like his calm play under pressure, making interceptions, anticipating danger and reading the game. When passing he always looks to play forward – breaking the lines in today’s parlance – and his passing accuracy is high. He is also forceful when moving with the ball and always aware of his distance to fellow defenders. Against Switzerland he was sent off for a last-ditch challenge to prevent a goal in the 80th minute and the opposition took full advantage, scoring a further three times, but as he walked off he could hold his head high.

His World Cup performances have captured a wider audience than he had last season in Scotland, where he delighted supporters of an improving Motherwell side with consistently high-quality displays. An intelligent middle-to-front forward, Just is a late developer. He previously played in Denmark and Austria after leaving New Zealand and is now showing a belief in his ability. Bigger defenders have been caught off balance by a quick body swerve as he moves with intent from the middle third into dangerous areas and at this tournament he has benefited from complementing the strength and hold-up play of Chris Wood. Just’s advantage over similar attacking midfielders is how quick he is to assess situations – he sees pictures. Twice against Iran he saw the space in which to receive from his target man and score with perfectly placed right-foot shots. He can score with his left too but needs to score more. Just is consistently a highly skilled performer at club level and shows a commendable humbleness and intelligence. If he continues his improvement he will be on a bigger club’s radar.

The introduction of the forward in the last minutes of the game against Bosnia and Herzegovina was quite dramatic. Within minutes this powerful, speedy, right-footed player destroyed his opponents’ hopes of surviving with a draw. They had just lost Muharemovic and Manzambi exploited the extra space with perfect timing to get two goals. When he scored the first, a well taken volley, it was clear he would be the centre of attention and it reminded me of the impact on Michael Owen’s life when he brushed past Argentina defenders to score for England in Saint-Étienne. Manzambi spent his early days with Servette before moving to Freiburg and has shown he has the pace and power, combined with adequate control, to trouble defenders in the Bundesliga. He seems well respected by his colleagues there but after contributing a combined 16 goals and assists for his club this season, he may soon have new teammates.

articles.title: US to probe petrol price gouging claims, Trump says
articles.summary: The president's remarks come as global oil prices have fallen but remain higher than before the US-Israel war with Iran.
articles.content:
US President Donald Trump has said he has ordered an investigation into major energy companies, accusing them of "gouging" customers by not cutting petrol prices after wholesale oil costs fell on global markets.

Trump wrote on social media that he has ordered the Department of Justice (DOJ) to "immediately start looking into this", adding he had expected to see petrol prices fall "a lot faster than what I'm seeing." He did not name any oil firms in the post.

His remarks come after the price of oil fell from peaks seen during the US-Israel war with Iran but remain higher than before the conflict started.

"The big Oil Companies are not dropping their price at the pump commensurate with the sharply lower prices they are paying for Oil," Trump said in the post.

"Those prices are dropping like a rock! In other words, customers are being 'gouged.'"

Oil prices shot up after Iran responded to US-Israeli strikes on 28 February by effectively shutting the critical Strait of Hormuz waterway , severely disrupting shipments of oil and gas and causing energy prices to soar.

Brent crude, the global wholesale oil benchmark, reached almost $120 (£91) a barrel in May as the war continued.

But prices have fallen since as peace talks have progressed. On Wednesday, Brent dropped below $76 a barrel, but it is still above the roughly $70 a barrel mark it was at before the conflict.

It is a similar picture with the US wholesale oil benchmark, WTI crude, which dipped under $72 a barrel on Wednesday but remains higher than before the war when it traded at around $60 a barrel.

Meanwhile, the average price of regular gasoline in the US has fallen to about $3.93 a gallon after topping $4 a gallon in April , its highest since 2022, but is still well above pre-war levels.

Trump's comments come after UK oil firms faced similar accusations of unfairly hiking petrol prices following the start of the Iran war.

However, the UK competition regulator said in May there was no widespread evidence of this , adding that average profit margins were "broadly unchanged" between February and March.
